abstracts.value: Data-driven machine learning algorithms represent an alternative to numerical or analytical modeling of vibrating objects for the purpose of extracting their material or geometric properties. Their performance is conditioned by the quality of the training dataset, which should contain all possible production configurations of the object and measurement conditions. In this work, we propose a data-augmentation method based on manipulations of the vibration properties rather than numerical signal post-processing. Instead of modifying the sample’s material or geometry, we connect an additional sensor and actuator to the sample and use low-latency electronics to control the feedback signal. This delivers an electromechanical system with tunable oscillation properties. This signal diversification method is demonstrated on the classification of correct and incorrect adhesion of two aluminum plates. The labeling accuracy of 67% on nine unknown test objects, when trained on a single unchangeable training object, increases to 83% when the variety of the training vibration signals is augmented by varying the parameters of the electrovibratory feedback. This provides advantages for industrial quality control, where a large number of reference training samples are not available.

titles.title: Data augmentation by an electro-vibratory feedback improves signal interpretation by neural networks

abstracts.value:
Recent studies have revealed that two-flavor u-d quark matter may serve as the true ground state of quantum chromodynamics (QCD). Meanwhile, a growing number of supermassive compact stars have been detected observationally, which brings severe challenges to explaining the internal matter composition of these compact objects. In this work, we systematically explore the parameter stability window of u-d quark matter within the enhanced perturbative QCD (EpQCD) model, and further investigate the structural properties of u-d quark stars under the framework of gravity’s rainbow theory.
By constructing a well-defined renormalization subtraction point, the EpQCD model successfully eliminates the thermodynamic inconsistency plaguing conventional perturbative QCD, and partially incorporates the global effect of quark confinement into the theoretical framework. As a quantum gravity candidate, gravity’s rainbow theory can effectively modify gravitational interactions inside compact stars via tuning rainbow function parameters, which provides a feasible theoretical scheme to account for extremely massive compact stars.
The left panel illustrates the stability window of u-d quark matter, while the right panel displays the mass-radius relation of u-d quark stars derived from gravity’s rainbow. The stability diagram indicates that the green stable parameter region is far narrower than the forbidden and phase-transition zones, yet absolute stable u-d quark matter is still theoretically achievable. Selecting representative parameters from the stable region, we compute the equilibrium structure of u-d quark stars and find that the maximum stellar mass rises monotonically with the rainbow function parameter Σ. Under the limit of standard general relativity (Ξ = Σ = 1), the maximum mass of a u-d quark star reaches 2.34 M⊙. Notably, when Σ = 1.2, the peak mass climbs to approximately 2.8 M⊙, consistent with the mass range of the compact companion in the GW190814 gravitational-wave event. Our results provide a novel perspective to interpret the intrinsic nature of ultra-massive compact stars, and advance our physical insights into the low-energy regime of quantum gravity.

titles.title: u-d Quark Matter in the Enhanced pQCD Model and u-d Quark Stars in Gravity’s Rainbow

abstracts.value: A new quench protection technique, energy shift with coupling (ESC), has recently been proposed, which is very promising for the protection of high-field magnets. The ESC system includes normal-conducting coils that are highly magnetically coupled to, but galvanically insulated from, the magnet coils. When the system is activated, rapid shift of energy from the magnet to the ESC coils is achieved, which quickly results in a substantial reduction of ohmic loss in the magnet hot spot and a transition of the superconducting coils to the normal state due to transient losses. Furthermore, during the magnet current discharge part of the magnet's stored energy is transferred to the ESC coils. ESC was recently successfully demonstrated at the European Council for Nuclear Research (CERN) on a 400 mm long flat racetrack in a structure without aperture. In this contribution, we present the application of the ESC method to a subscale common-coil magnet named subscale stress-managed common-coil series (subSMCC2), which was designed and manufactured by the magnet development laboratory at the Paul Scherrer Institute. The subSMCC2 is a 300 mm long magnet, including four stress-managed Nb<inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"><tex-math notation="LaTeX">$_{3}$</tex-math></inline-formula>Sn common-coils and designed to reach bore and coil peak fields of about 5.3 and 6.4 T, respectively, at a short-sample current of 9.5 kA. Protecting this magnet after a quench without using energy extraction is extremely difficult due to its very high stabilizer current density, which is higher than 5 kA/mm<inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"><tex-math notation="LaTeX">$^{2}$</tex-math></inline-formula>. The proposed ESC-based quench protection scheme relies on two ESC common-coil-type coils made of rectangular copper conductor, which are located on the outer sides of the magnet coils. Tests were carried out at the CERN magnet test facility, successfully demonstrating ESC performance under various operating conditions. These results show that ESC is an effective and high-performance technology that can protect magnets up to very high current densities.

A new quench-protection technique, energy shift with coupling (ESC), has recently been proposed and shows significant promise for the protection of high-field magnets. The ESC system includes normal-conducting coils that are strongly magnetically coupled to, but galvanically insulated from, the magnet coils. When activated, the system rapidly transfers energy from the magnet to the ESC coils, substantially reducing ohmic losses at the magnet hot spot and promoting the transition of the superconducting coils to the normal state through transient losses. During the subsequent magnet-current discharge, part of the stored magnetic energy is transferred to the ESC coils. ESC was recently demonstrated successfully at CERN on a 400 mm long flat racetrack magnet structure without an aperture. In this work, we present the application of the ESC method to a subscale common-coil magnet known as the subscale stress-managed common-coil series (subSMCC2), designed and manufactured by the Magnet Development Laboratory at the Paul Scherrer Institute. The subSMCC2 is a 300 mm long magnet comprising four stress-managed Nb₃Sn common coils and is designed to reach bore and peak coil fields of approximately 5.3 T and 6.4 T, respectively, at a short-sample current of 9.5 kA. Protecting this magnet following a quench, without the use of energy extraction, is particularly challenging because of its very high stabilizer current density, exceeding 5 kA/mm². The proposed ESC-based protection scheme employs two common-coil-type ESC coils made from rectangular copper conductors and located on the outer sides of the magnet coils. Tests performed at the CERN magnet test facility successfully demonstrated the performance of the ESC system under a variety of operating conditions. These results show that ESC is an effective, high-performance quench-protection technology capable of protecting magnets operating at very high current densities.

abstracts.value: Quantum computing based on photonic platforms offers a promising route toward scalable quantum information processing due to its low decoherence and access to high-dimensional state spaces. A promising approach for realizing photonic quantum computation is to encode quantum information in the Orbital Angular Momentum (OAM) states of light, enabling the realization of high-dimensional quantum gates. Implementing such quantum gates requires programmable unitary transformations between selected computational basis states. The fabrication of integrated multi-plane light conversion (MPLC) structures could provide a pathway toward large-scale programmable quantum processors. In this work, we investigate the implementation of photonic NOT-gate transformations using OAM states and MPLC systems with a limited number of phase planes. Unlike conventional MPLC approaches that optimize phase masks for a fixed modal basis, the proposed framework treats the computational basis itself as the optimization variable. To identify suitable computational basis states, a photonic quantum-gate optimization algorithm was developed to systematically evaluate candidate LG mode pairs. For each computational subspace, the three-plane MPLC phase masks were optimized using the wavefront-matching algorithm, and the corresponding modal and gate fidelities were calculated. The results show that conjugate-OAM mode pairs <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"><tex-math notation="LaTeX">${LG_{p}^{l},LG_{p}^{-l}}$</tex-math></inline-formula> and neighboring-radial mode pairs <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"><tex-math notation="LaTeX">${LG_{p}^{l},LG_{p+1}^{l}}$</tex-math></inline-formula> consistently achieve higher gate fidelity than structurally mismatched mode pairs under identical hardware constraints. These findings establish a direct relationship between computational-basis selection and quantum-gate performance, providing practical guidelines for computational-basis engineering in OAM-based quantum information processing, photonic quantum gates, and programmable quantum photonic processors.

titles.title: Photonic Quantum Gates Using OAM and MPLC

abstracts.value: Realistic simulation of quantum key distribution (QKD) networks requires a combination of precise models of quantum channels and network functions. Unfortunately, existing QKD network simulators lack either rigorous quantum physics modeling or network key-management and routing protocols, which limit their practical applicability. To address this limitation, we propose a QKD network simulator with hyperparameter tuning (QKDSim-HT), a NetSquid-based simulator specialized for polarization-based discrete-variable QKD networks. Specifically, QKDSim-HT models properties in quantum physics (photon loss, polarization-dependent depolarization, detector inefficiencies, dark counts, and dead times) as well as advanced functionalities in networking algorithms (multi-hop key relay and adaptive routing). Extensive simulations over diverse topologies reveal that the networking performance varied with respect to the fundamental properties of quantum physics, such as depolarization, fiber length, and channel attenuation. As a representative use case of QKDSim-HT, simulation results from QKDSim-HT over simple examples clearly manifest that a design of QKD networks highly affects performance of the networks. Accordingly, QKDSim-HT can serve as a practical platform for performance evaluation and optimization of quantum secured network.

titles.title: Quantum Key Distribution Network Simulator With Hyperparameter Tuning for Realistic Performance Analysis

abstracts.value: We present a unified theoretical framework for analyzing both electrostatic two-stream and electromagnetic Weibel instabilities in counterstreaming electron-positron pair plasmas. Through systematic derivation of dispersion relations in non-relativistic and relativistic regimes, we demonstrate how the symmetric mass ratio fundamentally alters instability characteristics compared to electron-ion systems. The two-stream instability, driven by longitudinal electrostatic perturbations parallel to beam motion, exhibits enhanced growth rates in pair plasmas due to equal contributions from both species, with relativistic suppression scaling as γ0−3 for both electrons and positrons. The Weibel instability, arising from transverse electromagnetic modes perpendicular to streaming directions, lacks the heavy-ion stabilization present in electron-ion plasmas, producing broader unstable spectral ranges and modified saturation levels. We derive explicit conditions determining the relative dominance of each mechanism across parameter space defined by drift velocity, wavenumber orientation, and relativistic Lorentz factor. Our analysis shows that longitudinal two-stream modes dominate at small perpendicular wavenumbers and moderate drift velocities, while transverse Weibel modes become prevalent at high perpendicular wavenumbers and large velocity spreads or temperature anisotropies. These findings have direct implications for understanding magnetic field generation, particle acceleration, and energy dissipation in astrophysical pair plasmas including pulsar wind nebulae, gamma-ray burst internal shocks, and active galactic nuclei jets where counterstreaming pair populations naturally arise.

titles.title: Suppression of two-stream and Weibel instabilities in ultra-relativistic electron–positron plasma

abstracts.value: Realistic quantum devices are open systems, and their behaviour depends not only on the subsystem of interest but also on how the environment is modelled and how the relevant observables are extracted. This thesis studies that problem in three settings. First, we study cavity-assisted qubit readout beyond the dispersive regime. We show that once coherent excitation exchange and dissipation become relevant, a microscopic treatment is needed to describe the readout quantitatively, and the optimal readout is set by a trade-off between signal accumulation and the distinguishability of the readout states. Second, we compare fermionic and spin baths in non-interacting transport models and show that spin baths reproduce fermionic reduced dynamics only in the large-bath weak-coupling limit, while clear deviations appear for smaller baths and near half-filling. Third, we study charge transport in molecular junctions using Automated Compression of Environments (ACE). There, the main difficulty is not the time evolution itself, but the extraction of the transport current, since this observable depends on system-environment correlations and is therefore not contained in the reduced system density matrix alone. We show that a probe-mode construction provides a viable route to reformulate the current as a system observable. This thesis advances our understanding of what is required for accurate modelling of open quantum dynamics across a range of solid-state settings, from cavity-assisted qubit readout to charge transport in molecular junctions.

titles.title: Developing and validating models of open quantum systems in solid-state nanostructures

abstracts.value: Using superconducting rectifiers to energize high-temperature superconducting (HTS) magnets is a promising approach to accelerate the uptake of HTS magnet technology. In this work, we start to address two limitations of the HTS superconducting rectifier concepts published to date; their low magnet charging voltages, and the variable properties of their HTS-based switches. Our approach is to test a centre-tapped full-wave transformer–rectifier utilizing HTS secondary windings and switch-arrays of Si <sc xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">mosfet</small>s mounted on a printed-circuit board (PCB). This approach has the advantage of greatly facilitating reproducible and reliable manufacture. The rectifier demonstrated magnet charging voltages exceeding a cycle-averaged 80 mV at 100 A and with typically more than 30% of the power supplied to the primary coils delivered to the magnet. We found it to be resilient to our preliminary thermal-cycling testing, with no degradation in performance observed over eight liquid-nitrogen to ambient (77–295 K) thermal cycles. We compare the impact of voltage- and current-controlled modes for the rectifier’s power supply. Our conclusion is that superconducting rectifiers using <sc xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">mosfet</small> switch arrays placed on PCBs is a very promising approach for low-current HTS magnet power supplies.

titles.title: Using Printed Circuit Boards and MOSFET Switch Arrays Toward the Reliable Manufacture of Superconducting Rectifiers

abstracts.value: Compact high turns ratio superconducting transformers are used to transfer power between low-current copper/ semiconductor-based circuits and high-current superconductor-based circuits. This type of transformer is a key component in devices, such as superconducting transformer rectifiers and superconducting current source inverters. Typically the copper winding and the superconducting winding are arranged with a turn ratio above 100:1, respectively, and are situated entirely within a cryogenic environment. The ohmic losses associated with the high count copper winding is problematic for most cryogenic applications and demands attention even when low currents on the order of 1–10 A are used. To address this problem, a transformer has been made using rare-earth barium copper oxide (REBCO) high-temperature superconductor (HTS) coated conductor for both the primary and secondary windings. The coupling coefficient and power consumption of this transformer were measured and compared to an equivalent transformer consisting of a copper primary winding and HTS secondary winding. The HTS primary was found to provide a significant reduction in transformer power consumption and a slight improvement to transformer coupling at frequencies below <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"><tex-math notation="LaTeX">$\sim$</tex-math></inline-formula>8 Hz. An increased transformer core loss and winding AC loss began to negate these efficiency improvements above <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"><tex-math notation="LaTeX">$\sim$</tex-math></inline-formula>8 Hz. In addition, cowinding the primary and secondary windings provided a higher coupling coefficient and lower power consumption for all winding combinations and frequencies tested. Finally, a short discussion on the implications of these findings respect to superconducting transformer rectifiers contextualizes the findings.

abstracts.value: This article investigates the mechanical characteristics and critical current performance of aluminum-stabilized stacked REBCO tape cable (ASTC) for the circular electron-positron collider detector magnet. In-plane bending, torsion, and uniaxial tension tests are carried out, combined by finite element analysis. The correlation between critical current and strain under different loading conditions is systematically analyzed, and key mechanical thresholds are determined. Results show that the minimum allowable in-plane bending diameter is 1200 mm. The critical twist pitch is 327 mm. The critical current degrades to 95% of the initial value when the tensile strain in the REBCO tape reaches 0.37%. This study provides essential experimental data and theoretical support for the structural design and engineering application of ASTC in high-field superconducting magnets.

abstracts.value: The study of quantum chromodynamics (QCD) at finite density remains one of the most formidable frontiers in the physics of strong interactions. QCD is strongly coupled at intermediate temperatures and densities, rendering perturbative techniques ineffective. Furthermore, first-principles calculations via lattice QCD, which have been highly successful at low densities, are fundamentally hindered by the numerical sign problem when describing dense matter. This leaves the properties of dense QCD matter, such as that produced in heavy-ion collisions or found in neutron stars, difficult to determine with conventional methods.Our research addresses these environments by utilizing the holographic principle, specifically the gauge/gravity duality, to investigate the strongly coupled dynamics of QCD. Originally developed in the context of string theory, the gauge/gravity duality, with the AdS/CFT correspondence as its canonical example, provides a dictionary that relates strongly coupled quantum field theories to gravitational theories in a higher-dimensional spacetime. The quantum field theory, which in our case models QCD, lives on the boundary of this spacetime. Within this framework, complicated problems regarding thermodynamic properties are translated into soluble geometric problems in the gravitational theory. In particular, we use black hole solutions of classical gravity to model the quark-gluon plasma. A central component of this work involves the development and refinement of bottom-up holographic models, which are phenomenologically constructed and tuned to reproduce key features of the boundary theory. Specifically, we focus on models based on the Einstein--Maxwell-dilaton and Dirac--Born--Infeld actions. These models are fitted to lattice QCD data at zero density and are then used to infer properties of QCD matter at finite density. Beyond investigating the transition between hadronic matter and the quark-gluon plasma, we also explore the potential for exotic states of matter that may emerge at finite density. This includes Higgs phases motivated by color superconductivity and spatially modulated inhomogeneous phases.The research offers model-based predictions for the location of the QCD critical point, where the line of first-order phase transitions terminates. We discuss our results in light of data from the Beam Energy Scan II program at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider. Furthermore, our findings suggest that dense matter near the critical point may not be homogeneous, but may instead exhibit spatial modulation, in a region of the phase diagram close to that probed experimentally. We also provide an example of how critical behavior depends on the flavor structure of the theory, and find that this behavior may be suppressed by the constraints on flavor composition present in heavy-ion collisions. These results provide new insights into the phase structure of dense QCD matter.

titles.title: Probing dense QCD with gauge/gravity duality

abstracts.value: <p>Axions are pseudoscalar particles that are a compelling addition to our theories of high-energy physics as they can solve two long-standing problems in modern physics. Firstly, cosmological and astrophysical observations indicate that the vast majority of the matter content of our universe is made of dark matter, a substance which cannot be described by the existing particles of the standard model of particle physics. A second major problem in modern physics is a lack of charge-parity (CP) symmetry violation in the strong force which could only arise from our current models through fine-tuning. The axion was initially proposed as a mechanism to naturally cancel the CP violation in the strong force, but it also proved to be a promising candidate for particle dark matter. Many experiments search for axion dark matter by measuring the conversion of axions into photons in a strong magnetic field. The Broadband Reflector Experiment for Axion Detection (BREAD) is one such experiment which uses a reflective surface to focus a photon signal onto an antenna or sensor. BREAD ultimately aims to search for axion-photon signals at frequencies as high as the infrared regime, but this work will focus on the instrumentation and analysis for a pilot version of BREAD which searched for axion-like particle and dark photon signals in a frequency range of 10.7 &minus;12.5 GHz. We will also discuss efforts to extend sensitivity of BREAD to the mm-wave range by, for example, exploiting a comb of resonant modes between a BREAD reflector and a secondary parabolic reflector. Finally, we discuss modeling of a supersymmetrized axion model and a sensitivity analysis of the ATLAS experiment to this model. While the axion-photon coupling is a relatively generic probe of axion models, there are some models, like the supersymmetric axion model introduced in this thesis, which can evade direct-detection axion-photon searches like BREAD. We will highlight the importance of complementing direct-detection experiments like BREAD with other probes of axion physics such as the collider sensitivity discussed here.</p>

titles.title: Broadening the Scope of Axion Searches: Reflector Haloscope Experiments for Broadband Axion Detection and Collider Probes of Supersymmetrized Axion Models

abstracts.value: <p>Precision cosmology experiments are ushering in an exciting era for fundamental physics by enabling searches for physics beyond the Standard Model and probing the extreme energy scales of the early Universe. Science cases such as identifying viable dark matter candidates, applying tighter constraints on the effective number of light relativistic species, and constraining cosmic birefringence are enabled by the deployment of increasingly sensitive Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) survey experiments like the Simons Observatory (SO). As experiments rapidly achieve large gains in sensitivity, the resolving factors of these ambitious science goals shift to the instrument&rsquo;s absolute calibrations such as its passbands and polarization angle.</p><p>In the first part of this thesis, I design, develop, and validate a novel bandpass calibrator with power variability that is capable of finely resolving bandpass edges. I then present material characterization of metamaterial anti-reflection cuttings and iron-loaded absorptive neutral density filters with varying concentrations that enable an extensive suite of in-lab testing and the necessary spectral corrections. This in-lab testing program is covered in the following chapter where we discuss the testing and integration of an SO small aperture telescope that housed a large aperture telescope&rsquo;s optics tube (&ldquo;camera&rdquo;). We fully populated the optical stack and carried out a range of testing to characterize and mitigate instrument systematics.</p><p>Finally, I discuss my work developing and fielding a bandpass calibrator for the SO small aperture telescopes. &nbsp;I design crossed-Dragonne style coupling optics and implement a mechanized design that permits scans over the full field-of-view of the telescope. Following in-lab testing and integration of the calibrator, we deploy it to the site and measure detector passbands. We confirm broad focal plane coverage and present preliminary passbands. We also offer a characterization of the SO small aperture telescope's polarization modulating half-wave plate's frequency dependence using these passbands. Future investigations are required to resolve a discrepancy with the expected performance. The half-wave plate's frequency dependent phase shift along with the passbands are necessary to properly calibrate the instrument's polarization angle for applications toward a probe of the parity-violating cosmic birefringence rotation angle, which is otherwise degenerate with the instrument's miscalibration angle.</p>

titles.title: Precision Calibration and Cosmic Birefringence with Simons Observatory

abstracts.value: The LHC produces an abundant flux of high-energy neutrinos and muons in the far-forward rapidity region. The neutrinos reach energies in the TeV range, which makes them the highest-energy neutrinos ever produced in a lab environment.In this thesis, scientific opportunities are explored to exploit the neutrino and muon flux to investigate the substructure of the proton. The impact of neutrino deep-inelastic scattering (DIS) measurements at the ongoing FASERν experiment and the planned detectors at the proposed Forward Physics Facility (FPF) on global Parton Distribution Function (PDF) extractions is assessed.A detailed phenomenological analysis of the DIS process is performed with state-of-the-art Monte Carlo simulation at next-to leading order in QCD expansion.This Monte Carlo simulation pipeline is then used to produce theory prediction that are required for a first machine-learning based extraction of the muon neutrino flux from FASER 2024 data. Fits of the neutrino flux allow to discriminate between different models of forward hadron production, constrain rare beyond the Standard Model decays to neutrinos and potentially provide evidence for the presence or absence of an intrinsic charm component of the proton.In the last part of the thesis, muon DIS is studied, which can probe the charm content of the proton directly, especially in the large-x region. This kinematic region is of special interest when searching for evidence for intrinsic charm. The analysis shows that the FASERν experiment could provide competitive constraints on intrinsic charm. Combining the FASERν emulsion detector with the electronic FASER detector it is also possible to construct a charm-asymmetry observable. A non-zero charm-asymmetrywould provide conclusive evidence for intrinsic charm

titles.title: Proton Structure and QCD under the LHC Neutrino Microscope

abstracts.value: Our future scientists and professionals must be conversant in computational techniques. In order to facilitate integration of computer methods into existing physics courses, Computational Problems for Physics offers a large number of worked examples and problems with fully guided solutions in Python (as well as Mathematica, Java, C, Fortran, and Maple on the Web). The book can be used as a self-study guide for learning how to use computer methods in physics. abstracts.value: Quantum Matters: From Field to Life bridges the gap between the mysterious world of quantum physics and the technologies that shape our daily lives. This innovative book takes readers on a comprehensive journey from fundamental quantum principles to their real-world applications, revealing how the invisible rules governing the smallest particles power everything from global positioning system (GPS) navigation and magneticresonance imaging (MRI) scans to the emerging quantum revolution in computing, communication, and medicine. Rather than treating quantum science as an abstract academic subject, this book demonstrates how quantum mechanics is already woven into the fabric of modern society and explores how quantum technologies promise to transform industries, secure communications, and unlock new possibilities in energy, healthcare, and beyond.This book's unique strengths include its interdisciplinary approach that connects quantum principles across physics, materials, engineering, biology, medicine, and finance, making complex concepts accessible without sacrificing depth. It features clear explanations of everyday quantum technologies like smartphones, lasers, and atomic clocks, showing readers the hidden quantum science behind familiar devices. The text provides comprehensive coverage of emerging quantum frontiers including quantum computing, cryptography, and sensing, while exploring the fascinating field of quantum biology and its role in photosynthesis and animal navigation. Additionally, it offers global perspective on quantum innovation, highlighting international investments and collaborations that are shaping the quantum ecosystem, all presented through an engaging narrative style that combines scientific accuracy with inspiring storytelling.This book serves a diverse readership including graduate students across multiple disciplines who need to understand quantum science's relevance to their fields; interdisciplinary professionals in engineering, computing, biology, and finance seeking practical insights; and curious general readers interested in cutting-edge science. For educators and policymakers, it provides essential context for understanding the strategic importance of quantum technologies in the global economy.  Whether you're a student building foundational knowledge, a professional exploring quantum applications in your industry, or simply someone fascinated by how science shapes the future, Quantum Matters empowers you to see quantum science not as distant theory but as a transformative force already shaping today's world and tomorrow's possibilities.

abstracts.value: Cosmic inflation is a period of accelerated expansion in the early universe which generates the primordial perturbations that lead to structure formation in the late universe.These perturbations are also imprinted on the cosmic microwave background (CMB) and can be parametrised by the spectral index of the scalar perturbations $n_s$ and the tensor-to-scalar ratio $r$, which were measured by the Planck mission, the BICEP/Keck experiments, and by the ACT and SPT experiments.These observables probe energies beyond the reach of terrestrial experiments, and they are sensitive not only to the matter content driving inflation, but also to the underlying theory of gravity.In the metric formulation of general relativity, the connection is a priori assumed to be the Levi--Civita connection.In the metric-affine (or Palatini) formulation, both the metric and the connection are independent variables, and the gravitational degrees of freedom can be carried by nonmetricity and torsion as well as curvature.For the Einstein--Hilbert action with minimally coupled matter the two formulations coincide, but once the inflaton couples non-minimally to the curvature, or higher-order curvature terms are included, they define different theories. The formulation of gravity is then a physical question to be settled by observation.In this thesis we study how inflaton-coupled modifications of gravity in the Palatini formulation predict different CMB observables in three distinct theories and three geometric assumptions. For the unconstrained connection, and when either torsion or nonmetricity is set to zero, we consider: the Chern--Simons term, the Gauss--Bonnet term, and independent distortion terms.In all three studies the modification sources the distortion, which we integrate out to alter the inflaton kinetic term. This reshapes the potential and the predictions for $n_s$ and $r$. The observables may thus discriminate between modifications of gravity, and between the a priori assumptions made about the connection.Forthcoming experiments such as the Simons Observatory and LiteBIRD will sharpen the constraints on $n_s$ and $r$, and probe the theory of gravity underlying inflation.

titles.title: Inflation in Metric-affine Modified Gravity

abstracts.value: <jats:p>We examine the family-separated seesaw (FSS) ansatz proposed in arXiv:2605.27049v2. Combining its paired cancellations with exact partial unitarity fixes the light and heavy mixing blocks in terms of one unitary matrix and the paired mass ratios. We classify their unitary completions and reconstruct the Dirac and singlet Majorana mass matrices, distinguishing the physical heavy masses from the singlet mass parameters. This identifies FSS as an exact realization of form dominance whose conventional one-loop leptogenesis cancellation is already established. The particular sum of lepton-number-violating invariants entering the proposed decay asymmetry therefore vanishes; individual CP invariants need not vanish. We also correct the heavy-mass reconstruction formulas and quantify their errors for both light-mass orderings. These formulas are conditional algebraic relations, not independent predictions of the heavy spectrum. Numerical mass–mixing illustrations, explicit chiral projections for double-beta decay, and a leading-logarithmic estimate of radiative misalignment clarify the physical reach and limitations. The contribution is an exact consistency analysis and correction of specific proposed consequences rather than a new mass-generation mechanism or a general prohibition of leptogenesis.</jats:p>

titles.title: On Family-Separated Seesaw Relations: Exact Reconstruction and Corrections

abstracts.value: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires classical decoders that can keep up with syndrome data streams and supply correction information and logical measurement outcomes to the quantum control system. Meeting these requirements at scale requires high throughput while controlling the end-to-end latency from readout to usable correction. In this paper, we organize decoding algorithms, execution strategies, and code constructions using common classifications and examine their performance and trade-offs under the reported evaluation conditions. We distinguish decoder-level hierarchy, where multiple decoding stages or resources cooperate to decode a single code, from code-level hierarchy, where the code construction itself introduces multiple decoding levels. We first review single-code hierarchical decoders and their cascaded predecoding and windowed, streaming, and distributed implementations. We then study hierarchical and concatenated codes, focusing on how decoding is coordinated across code levels through hard decisions, soft reliability information, or syndrome information. We also examine how qubit modalities shape decoding workloads and timing requirements, and review how different decoding platforms meet these requirements, including central processing units (CPUs), graphics processing units (GPUs), field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs), application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs), and cryogenic platforms. By assessing design trade-offs, this paper clarifies connections across the literature and provides a shared foundation for QEC design exploration. It also identifies gaps in performance reporting and system integration to guide future research toward practical quantum error correction.

titles.title: Hierarchical Decoding for Quantum Error Correction

abstracts.value: Motivated by quantum key distribution networks, we compare key relay protocols with secure network coding on the same undirected graph. In this comparison, we fix the finite field, terminal set, and wiretap family. Each edge supplies one independent uniform symbol to its endpoints for key relay, or carries one symbol once for network coding. The network code may choose its source terminal, edge orientations, and causal transmission order before execution. In this setting, the standard one-time-pad simulation readily converts every secure network code to key relay. We investigate the reverse conversion to linear network coding. For two terminals and a one-symbol key, arbitrary key relay is equivalent to scalar linear acyclic network coding over the prescribed field. The proof uses connectivity and flow conservation, related to the binary $st$-flow protocol. However, this equivalence fails in general when several terminals seek one common key. A doubled triangle separates key relay from acyclic coding but admits causal coding on a cyclic orientation. On the four-terminal complete graph, a linear key relay protocol over the ternary field withstands the three perfect-matching wiretap sets, whereas no linear causal network code distributes a source symbol of the same size, even with private randomness at every vertex and its use in decoding. We also establish a linear key relay normal form that removes interaction and private randomness and bounds public communication. All results concern one-shot feasibility with exact agreement and perfect secrecy.

titles.title: Key Relay and Secure Network Coding: One-Shot Equivalence and Separation on Undirected Networks

abstracts.value:
We study exact quantum algorithms for block compositions of total Boolean functions. For an outer function $f$ of degree $D$ and an inner function $g$ on $m$ bits, we prove 
$$ Q_E(f\circ g)=O\!\left(mD+Q_E(f)Q_{1/(4D)}(g)\right). $$
 The algorithm combines approximate inner evaluations with a finite exact correction. Its two costs are governed by different parameters of the outer function: exact query complexity determines the cost of simulation, whereas polynomial degree determines the number of inner blocks used in the correction. We first establish the construction with an arity-dependent error threshold and then obtain the degree-dependent threshold above. For recursive ternary not-all-equal, this gives an exact algorithm using $(3/\sqrt2)^{k(1+o(1))}$ queries asymptotically. More generally, for every fixed nonconstant total gadget $h$, we determine the exact recursive rate as $\max\{\textrm{deg}(h),\operatorname{Adv}^{\pm}(h)\}$ and prove $Q_E(h^{\circ k})=\widetilde O_h(R(h^{\circ k})^2)$. The composition limit also allows to transfer separations from $Q_{\varepsilon}$ and $°$ to exact quantum query complexity $Q_E$ (similar to fractional block sensitivity to block sensitivity transfer in Tal and Kulkarni 2016, Chicago Journal of Theoretical Computer Science). We construct a family with $s=\operatorname{bs}=\operatorname{fbs}\ge Q_E^{3/2-o(1)}$, improving the previous exponent $1.1527\ldots$. A second construction gives $R \ge Q_E^{2-o(1)}$, improving the previous exponent $3/2$. We also allow different inner functions and give analogous quantitative separations in quantum communication.

titles.title: Exact Quantum Algorithms for Composed Boolean Functions

abstracts.value: A large body of work in quantum machine learning has centered on characterizing the expressivity and performance of quantum models. In contrast, little attention has been paid to the reliability of predictions beyond average performance measures such as accuracy. In this work, we introduce an uncertainty-aware quantum classification framework based on Dempster-Shafer theory. This theory allows to express uncertainty through weights assigned not only to individual classification labels but to sets of labels. We introduce a training strategy that enables parameterized quantum circuits to learn such assignments directly from data. This provides an efficient way to prepare the corresponding quantum states and enables the application of different post-processing strategies. In particular, it offers a practical setting for quantum Dempster-Shafer fusion procedures with polynomial resource requirements, even when the corresponding mass functions are defined over exponentially many subsets. Overall, our work represents a step toward enabling quantum models to express uncertainty about their predictions, thereby extending the evaluation of quantum models beyond predictive performance alone.

titles.title: Uncertainty-aware quantum machine learning based on Dempster-Shafer theory

abstracts.value: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires quantum error-correction (QEC) decoders that achieve low logical error rates under real-time operating constraints. These constraints motivate heuristic decoding algorithms whose error-correction performance must be evaluated through large-scale simulation. High-throughput decoding accelerates this evaluation and the exploration of decoder parameters. Using multiple graphics processing units (GPUs) is a natural way to scale these simulations, but naively distributing syndrome batches introduces host-side preprocessing and output-collection overheads that limit scaling. To address these limitations, we extend the Pêlagos relay belief-propagation (Relay-BP) decoder with process-isolated orchestration, parallel host preprocessing, and shared-memory output. We evaluate both one-gross ($[[144,12,12]]$) and two-gross ($[[288,12,18]]$) codes in a multi-GPU environment. Specifically, for the one-gross circuit at $R=50$, eight AMD Instinct MI300X GPUs and eight AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs achieve optimized end-to-end speedups of $5.68\times$ and $6.23\times$, respectively. For the two-gross circuit, the corresponding speedups are $6.92\times$ and $7.01\times$. When throughput is calculated using GPU decoding time, the corresponding two-gross speedups are $7.58\times$ and $7.45\times$, indicating near-linear GPU scaling. We deploy Pêlagos on Lux, Oak Ridge National Laboratory's AMD Instinct MI355X-based supercomputer, as a pathfinding application for high-throughput QEC simulation. This deployment provides a concrete quantum-computing use case for the AI + HPC infrastructure supporting the Genesis Mission's scientific-discovery goals. These end-to-end measurements demonstrate a practical path to accelerating large-scale QEC simulation through efficient multi-GPU decoding.

titles.title: Scaling Pêlagos: Multi-GPU Orchestration for Relay Belief-Propagation Decoding

abstracts.value: Frequency-domain multiplexing is a fundamental technology for readout of cryogenic detector arrays on a single transmission line. Synthesizing a large number of static carrier tones for resonator stimulation eventually drives the cryogenic low-noise amplifier beyond its P1dB, introducing detector signal distortion. Scaling array sizes to O(10^6) detector pixels therefore demands minimizing the total power on the transmission line by continuous tracking of the resonances, which requires the readout electronics to be capable of updating the carrier tones dynamically. This work presents an scalable FPGA-based implementation for carrier signal synthesis based on a numerically controlled oscillator and a polyphase filter bank, enabling real-time frequency adaptivity as well as frequency resolution of 4 mHz to precisely tune the operating point, while simultaneously reducing resource usage compared to the current memory-based implementation.

titles.title: Adaptive carrier signal synthesis for frequency-division multiplexed cryogenic detector readout

abstracts.value: Large language models (LLMs) have recently demonstrated the ability to generate parameters for variational quantum circuits without conventional optimization. However, the conditions under which this approach is effective remain unclear. Here, we investigate a frozen, general-purpose LLM that generates complete circuit parameter vectors from symbolic circuit and Hamiltonian descriptions, with optional iterative energy feedback. We evaluate the approach on general random Hamiltonians, structured parent Hamiltonians, and molecular systems. For general Hamiltonians, LLM-generated parameters exhibit larger energy errors than conventional Adam optimization, while additional feedback generally provides limited improvement. In contrast, for structured Hamiltonians, the LLM can generate promising low-energy parameter configurations, suggesting that identifiable physical and mathematical structure facilitates parameter inference. We also show that direct LLM predictions of minimum energies can violate the Hamiltonian spectral lower bound, whereas generated circuit parameters allow independent evaluation of physically realizable energy expectation values. Finally, we investigate blind circuit interpretation and find that the LLM can predict measurement outcomes even when it fails to identify the underlying quantum algorithm. These findings highlight the role of problem structure, the limitations of iterative LLM optimization, and the importance of independently verifiable predictions in quantum parameter programming.

titles.title: Programming Quantum Circuit Parameters with Large Language Models

abstracts.value: A normalized two-point function with several poles does not, on its own, fix the source-free thermal partition function. For the Gaussian measure of the original gluon field, a positive-residue rational propagator contributes determinants from its poles and from zeros interlaced between them. The zero factors distinguish this completion from a gas of independent pole fields and restore two ultraviolet polarizations per adjoint eigenvalue at every finite truncation. We apply the construction to a background-covariant completion of the elliptic Dyson-Schwinger gluon kernel. The first-order SU(3) transition is already present with a single pole, and the saturated six-pole result shifts $T_c/M_g$ by only $1.48\%$, where $T_c$ is the coexistence temperature and $M_g$ is the lowest pole mass. At six poles, the zero determinants raise $T_c/M_g$ by $2.31\%$ and lower $L/T_c^4$ by $12.4\%$, where $L$ is the latent heat and each prescription uses its own $T_c$. At fixed $M_g$ the dimensional latent heat decreases by $4.0\%$. The fixed-holonomy free-energy difference gives an ultraviolet test independent of the additive pressure normalization. At fixed pole number $P$, its asymptotic value agrees with the two-polarization Weiss result when the zeros are retained and is $(3P-1)/2$ times as large in the poles-only prescription.

titles.title: Poles Are Not Enough: Zeros of Dyson-Schwinger Gluon Propagators in Yang-Mills Thermodynamics

abstracts.value: We develop a spinorial symmetry framework for metric Dirac structures in $H$-twisted exact Courant algebroids. A generalized metric equips a Dirac structure with an intrinsic Riemannian Lie-algebroid geometry and identifies it isometrically with the positive subbundle of the generalized tangent bundle. For sections preserving the generalized metric, we prove an exact intertwining between the positive-spinor Kosmann--Dorfman action and the intrinsic Kosmann derivative. The comparison is independent of the auxiliary compatible generalized connection. Within the intrinsic geometry we derive Killing--Yano (KY) and conformal Killing--Yano (CKY) integrability identities, construct Killing-spinor-preserving operators from odd special KY and even special closed CKY forms, and obtain these forms from Hermitian bilinears of Killing spinors with imaginary Killing number. We illustrate the framework on a global Dirac structure over $S^2\times S^1$ with nontrivial $H$-flux class and rank-two anchor. Its spin connection and symmetry operators are explicit, and its Killing-spinor space is a transverse family $C^\infty(S^1,\mathbb C^2)$. Finally, intrinsic Killing sections act on Killing spinors by a Lie algebra representation. For a graph Dirac structure over $S^3$, the odd Jacobi identity of the Hermitian-current bracket fails by a phase, and adjoining a single even phase generator yields a Lie superalgebra. These results connect generalized isometries, hidden spinorial symmetries, and flux-sensitive Lie-algebroid geometry.

titles.title: Generalized Kosmann derivative and symmetry operators on Dirac structures

abstracts.value: We develop a first-principles framework for analyzing photonic quantum communication in an atomic medium. Starting from a real-space quantization of the electromagnetic field coupled to an ensemble of two-level atoms, we derive an effective model for polarization-encoded single-photon states. We apply this framework to superdense coding to study communication efficiency and to the BB84 quantum key distribution protocol for communication security. For superdense coding, we evaluate the protocol capacity of the fixed Bell-state alphabet under erasure, dephasing, and depolarizing channels and show that it decreases monotonically with increasing atom-field coupling. For BB84, we formulate a modified protocol that discards erasure outcomes and uses the microscopic model to estimate the intrinsic loss rate. We derive the corresponding asymptotic key rate and show that it decreases monotonically with coupling strength and vanishes beyond a finite critical coupling.

titles.title: Effect of atomic interactions on quantum communication protocols

abstracts.value: Let $V^{\Bbbk}(\mathfrak{g})$ be the universal affine vertex algebra attached to a finite-dimensional complex simple Lie algebra at arbitrary level, and let $M=\bigoplus_{N=0}^{\infty}M_N$ be a $V^{\Bbbk}(\mathfrak{g})$ -module. We give an explicit formula for every genus-one trace of affine currents as a finite sum over cycle partitions. We then show the convergence of all fixed zero-mode trace series, hence absolute locally uniform convergence of the current traces and their meromorphic continuation on the elliptic configuration space. The same conclusion is obtained for arbitrary affine-state insertions. Finally, we compute the cases of at most four currents and the nodal limit $q\to 0$, in which the type-1 and type-2 elliptic cycle coefficients degenerate to rational genus-zero cycle coefficients and the module trace reduces to the ground-state space.

titles.title: Affine Vertex Operator Algebras and Correlation Functions on Elliptic Curves

abstracts.value: We study inequalities between symmetric functions that hold in every number of variables. First, we prove that it is undecidable whether a symmetric function with rational coefficients is nonnegative in all dimensions, answering a question posed by Acevedo, Blekherman, Debus and Riener. As a consequence, the validity of dimension-free moment criteria for entanglement in quantum information is undecidable. Second, we present a homogeneous symmetric function of degree 8 which is positive definite in every dimension but admits no sum of squares multiplier that is uniform in the number of variables. Consequently, Artin's solution of Hilbert's 17th problem and the Krivine-Stengle Positivstellensatz have no any-dimensional analog and any-dimensional Positivstellensätze asked for by Levin and Chandrasekaran cannot hold in general.

titles.title: Hilbert's 17th problem for symmetric functions: undecidability and a counterexample

abstracts.value: We investigate inducing data for three dimensional asymptotically flat BMS gravity on hyperbolic Virasoro orbits with winding, which contain no constant supermomentum, and the restriction of formal smooth equivariant sections to global Lorentz orbits. Using the developing map of the associated Hill operator we rederive their stabilizer and show that, in the spin double cover, it is the direct product of a line with a cyclic group of even order. The character of the cyclic factor is therefore a discrete inducing label independent of the continuous one, unlike for the massive BMS particles, where it is fixed by the spin. At points with the corresponding finite rotational symmetry, restriction of formal smooth equivariant sections to a global Lorentz orbit yields the finite cyclic equivariance condition, while an independently defined unitary global branch realizes the associated finite difference equation. At points with timelike projected momentum we derive the resulting ladder of Poincare helicities, show that the projected rest energy is not an orbit invariant, construct locally flat winding BMS geometries with hyperbolic Lorentz holonomy, prove that the smooth real periodic near horizon current model excludes these winding orbits, and obtain selection rules and closed form expressions for finite monodromy resolved orbital functionals. A unitary realization on the full infinite dimensional orbit is not constructed, and the interpretation of the cyclic sectors in quantum gravity remains conjectural.

titles.title: Finite cyclic monodromy in BMS3 gravity

abstracts.value: How well a superposition of nonorthogonal states, such as an optical cat state, serves as a resource depends on how its components interfere. Here we determine the optimal probability of converting one such superposition into another by superposition-free operations. These operations cannot make the components of a superposition interfere more destructively with certainty while keeping all of them, and this principle fixes the optimal probability for every source that is symmetric under permutations of its components. When the reference states are coherent states, as in a cat state, every operation that maps each of them to a coherent state, such as photon loss or photon subtraction, is superposition-free. For two reference states we solve the problem completely. Superpositions with coefficients of equal modulus, the counterparts of the maximally coherent states of coherence theory, are therefore inequivalent resources: an odd cat state becomes even with certainty by a normalized photon subtraction, whereas an even one becomes odd only with a probability that vanishes for small amplitudes, and the even and the Yurke$-$Stoler cat states cannot be converted into each other with certainty in either direction. Collective operations on several copies can do better than converting them one at a time, except in the distillation of coherence, which gains nothing from them. For three or more reference states with equal positive overlaps, no state reaches every other state with certainty; the equal-modulus superpositions that interfere most destructively still yield a maximally coherent state with certainty and reach every superposition of all reference states at least as well as such a state does, but in the worst case no better.

titles.title: Probabilistic distillation of superposition

abstracts.value: We give a rigorous, constructive proof that there exists a Ricci-flat Kähler metric on the Fermat quartic hypersurface, independently of Yau's famous theorem, along with an explicit and accurate analytic approximation to the metric. The proof combines numerical techniques to obtain the approximately Ricci flat metric, a fixed point theorem to prove existence, and verified numerics to get the bounds used by the fixed point theorem. The method is general and we discuss the computational issues in applying it to other manifolds.

titles.title: A constructive computer-assisted existence proof for a Calabi--Yau metric

abstracts.value: We show that the domain of outer communications of a smooth, asymptotically flat, stationary vacuum spacetime describing a single rotating non-degenerate black hole is isometric to the domain of outer communications of a subextremal Kerr solution under reasonable geometric and physical assumptions, without analyticity or any smallness assumptions. The method is to apply Harrison transform to construct a family of solutions of Einstein--Maxwell equations. Combining null area comparison with the area-charge inequality, we show that, in the limiting transformed geometry, the bifurcate sphere has area radius one and constant electric and magnetic flux densities, with the original ADM mass normalized to $M=1$. These identities imply the technical assumptions of Ionescu--Klainerman, yielding the identification with Kerr.

titles.title: The uniqueness of smooth stationary black holes

abstracts.value: We introduce a geometric construction whose terminal configuration determines the kernel and cokernel of a morphism between positive Lagrangian branes in the derived Fukaya category of a Calabi-Yau manifold. Thus, if the construction always terminates, the full subcategory of positive Lagrangian branes is abelian, as conjectured by Joyce. We show that this abelian category admits Harder-Narasimhan filtrations with respect to the central charge defined by the holomorphic volume form. Under appropriate split-generation assumptions, we construct a Bridgeland stability condition whose stable objects are isomorphic to special Lagrangian branes, as predicted by the Thomas-Yau conjecture. The geometric construction is based on a one-parameter family of special Lagrangian submanifolds with boundary. One part of the boundary is contained in the Lagrangian underlying the domain of the morphism and the other in the Lagrangian underlying the codomain. Surgeries occur as the family encounters singularities or obstruction walls. We prove that the construction always terminates for the two-torus and provide higher dimensional examples.

titles.title: Toward the abelian category of positive Lagrangians

abstracts.value: We study quantum Hamiltonians whose separated angular component is expressed through a generic Painlevé VI transcendent. We construct generalized ladder operators for one-dimensional Schrödinger operators with a quadratic spectral variable. For the Painlevé VI angular Hamiltonian these operators satisfy $[N,J_\pm]=\pm2kJ_\pm$, where $N=\sqrt M$, and close through an eighth-degree norm polynomial. Combining the angular shifts with the radial shift operators of the oscillator, Coulomb and free Bessel systems yields higher-order integrals and deformed Racah-type polynomial algebras for the two-dimensional superintegrable models. This construction provides new families of Tremblay-Turbiner-Winternitz (TTW)- and Post-Winternitz (PW)-like Hamiltonians with integrals of arbitrarily high order and Painlevé VI in the potential. This framework also recovers models from the classification of third- and fourth-order integrals as particular cases. For a representative oscillator extension we compute the Casimir explicitly and recover the finite-dimensional energy spectrum from a deformed-oscillator realization. We then analyze the special-solution sector using the explicit families collected by Gromak, Laine and Shimomura. The resulting potentials are organized into a small number of spectral classes, and the distinction between formal zeros of the ladder norm and physical self-adjoint representations is made explicit. The regular nonclassical rational examples are rational Darboux deformations of the trigonometric Pöschl--Teller system and lead to strictly isospectral exceptional-Jacobi sectors or to state-adding representations with an isolated angular level. A singular branch produces an interior inverse-square barrier and a split-domain problem. For one regular exceptional sector and two state-adding sectors we display the polynomial algebras.

abstracts.value: Motivated by the conjectural relationship between the IKKT matrix model and type IIB string theory, we classify supersymmetric twists of the matrix model, allowing for both dynamical and kinematical supercharges. Beyond the two twists available at any finite $N$, which we studied in our previous work, we find five additional classes at infinite rank which require non-commuting backgrounds associated with D-branes in IIB supergravity. Together, these twists realize representatives of every equivalence class of twisting supercharges in flat-space type IIB supergravity recently classified by the first author; however, the precise form of the orbit stratification differs. This difference is related to a higher central extension of the IIB superalgebra that appears in our treatment of the IKKT model in the BV formalism. Expanding around the non-commutative backgrounds gives worldvolume theories on products of A- and B-branes, including four-dimensional BF theory on an emergent D3-brane. We relate all these twists to deformations of BCOV theory (the closed string field theory of the topological B-model) using the open-closed duality of classical string field theory. For one of the twists with Spin$(7)$ symmetry, we also show the localization of the IKKT partition function by Moore, Nekrasov, and Shatashvili can be directly reconstructed with the BV formalism, with their auxiliary field completion encoded by quadratic antifield terms. abstracts.value: Multiparameter pure-state metrology is limited by the incompatibility of measurements optimized for different parameters. We characterize uniform sensitivity by the Fisher floor, the smallest fraction of the quantum Fisher information (QFI) retained over all pure states and parameter directions. We prove that a constant number of fixed orthonormal bases suffices for a nearly optimal Fisher floor, independently of the Hilbert-space dimension $d$. With high probability, five independent Haar bases already achieve a positive, dimension-independent floor, and larger constant families achieve approximate universal Fisher symmetry: they retain nearly one half of the QFI in every direction, the largest uniform fraction permitted by measurement incompatibility. The required number of bases is optimal up to a logarithmic factor in inverse accuracy. In contrast, $d+1$ mutually unbiased bases, when they exist, can minimize mean Fisher anisotropy among families of $d+1$ bases yet have a Fisher floor of at most $1/(d+1)$, showing that optimal average balance does not ensure uniform sensitivity.

abstracts.value: We present a pair of spinorial equations, generalizing the internal Killing spinor equations of Type I supergravity, and show that they characterize several classes of Bismut-Hermitian-Einstein structures on six-dimensional Riemannian spin manifolds. We show that in this framework the local reduction to a four-dimensional transverse Hermitian geometry is provided by two canonical, commuting, Bismut-parallel Killing vector fields arising as bilinears in the Killing spinors, without assuming compactness. In one class, the transverse geometry is conformally Kahler and both compact and non-compact solutions exist. We also discuss variants that do not admit compact solutions, one of which has hyper-Hermitian transverse geometry. We discuss the relation of these structures to the Hull-Strominger system with closed three-form and to five-dimensional Gauntlett-Kim geometries and provide explicit embeddings in Type I, Type IIB and massive Type IIA supergravity, as well as in generalized supergravity. We illustrate our results with a number of examples, both compact and non-compact.

abstracts.value: We develop a metriplectic framework for quantum--classical hybrid dynamics that ensures thermodynamic consistency through conservation of energy and non-negative entropy production. The approach combines a hybrid Poisson bracket with a metriplectic $4$-bracket, with coupling between quantum and classical subsystems arising solely through dissipative processes. Within this hybrid formulation, we produce thermodynamically consistent generalizations of the Lindblad master equations and the Bloch--Torrey equations for open quantum systems. This provides a unified description of quantum relaxation and classical diffusion, together with a clear interpretation of entropy production.

abstracts.value: The question of local encodability asks: can a given, multipartite pure quantum state be completed to an orthonormal basis using only local unitary rotations? If any such state in a given system has this property, it is called universally locally encodable (ULE), a feature, which has applications in quantum information theory, engineering and math. Despite its easy formulation, the answer to this question depends nontrivially on the local dimensions of the system: While universal local encodability is known for $2\times 2$, $4\times 4$ and $8\times 8$-dimensional systems, it was so-far only conjectured to hold in $3\times 3$, and non-ULE was recently proved for systems of four and more qubits by Pauwels and Gühne. We resolve the open conjecture by proving universality for two qutrits. Furthermore, we construct (among others) universal local encodings in dimensions $d\times2$ for $d\ge2$, in dimensions $d\times3$ for $d=3,4$ and $d\ge6$, and in every bipartite system with one or two infinite-dimensional subsystems. For finite-dimensional multipartite systems, we turn a heuristic parameter count into a necessary condition for universality, which excludes universal local encodability in infinitely many cases. Finally, we give universal local encodability an operational interpretation by showing that non-ULE is equivalent to whether general measurements yield an advantage over projectively simulable ones in discrimination tasks where unknown, random local unitary rotations have to be detected.

titles.title: When can local unitaries generate a complete orthogonal basis?

abstracts.value: We investigate multiparameter quantum metrology and the energetic properties of an effective electron--proton spin system inspired by the hyperfine structure of the hydrogen atom. Considering the external magnetic field $\mathcal B$ and the hyperfine coupling strength $Λ$ as unknown parameters, we derive the quantum Fisher information matrix and establish the corresponding quantum Cramér--Rao bounds for their simultaneous estimation. We analyze the estimation precision and the correlations between the two parameters, showing that the weak-commutativity condition is satisfied despite the noncommutativity of the associated symmetric logarithmic derivatives. Independently, we explore the energetic properties of the system under a unitary charging protocol, characterizing its ergotropy, anti-ergotropy, storage capacity, and energy-basis coherence. We investigate the dependence of these quantities on the magnetic field, hyperfine coupling, temperature, and charging time. Our results provide a comprehensive characterization of the metrological properties and energetic performance of a hyperfine spin-based quantum system, highlighting its potential as a platform for quantum sensing and energy storage.

abstracts.value: Crossing a domain wall can permute anyons, and intersecting strings can create a particle. These couplings between defects of various dimensions are specified by higher groups. We develop a lattice framework defining higher-group statistics as Berry phases of closed sequences of hopping operators, invariant under local modifications of the operators. Our central example is a closed Majorana chain, a 1-dimensional topological superconductor, embedded in 3 dimensions. We construct a loop-flip process with phase $+i$, refining the usual $\pm 1$ loop-flip invariant through intermediate transfer of fermion parity between the chain and physical fermions. In two dimensions, charge-wall statistics distinguish two $\mathbb Z_4$ toric codes enriched by $\mathbb Z_2$ charge-conjugation symmetry, with identical anyon statistics but distinct gauged theories: the quantum doubles of the dihedral group $D_4$ and the quaternion group $Q_8$. We provide two complementary constructions of statistical processes. The first extends the Smith normal form algorithm in [Phys. Rev. X $\textbf{16}$, 011010 (2026), arXiv:2412.01886] to higher groups, generating processes from lattice geometry and prescribed local moves. For a finite higher group $\mathbb G$, we prove that statistical processes on a $d$-sphere are classified by $H_{d+2}(B\mathbb G,\mathbb Z)$. The second constructs processes directly from homology classes without examining exponentially many defect configurations, enabling us to study statistics for complex higher-group structures where the previous method is computationally prohibitive. These processes detect boundary anomalies of higher-group symmetry-protected topological phases. For example, we distinguish 2-group anomalies in 1, 2, and 3 dimensions. Higher-group statistics provide new invariants for characterizing coupled defects in quantum many-body systems.

titles.title: Higher-Group Statistics on Lattices

abstracts.value: We solve the Cauchy problem for an irreducible real spinor parallel with respect to a metric connection with skew-symmetric torsion on a globally hyperbolic Lorentzian four-manifold, proving that it is well-posed modulo an obstruction that we identify explicitly, and obtaining an initial-data characterization of such spinors. Our proof relies on the theory of spinorial forms, which we use to explicitly integrate the coupled flow for the spinor and underlying metric via a rotated pull-back action of the flow generated by a vector field on the Cauchy hypersurface $Σ$. We characterize the corresponding constraint equations as an explicit exterior differential system and describe all its solutions in terms of contact structures and flat foliations, obtaining a complete classification in the compact case. In particular, we conclude that every oriented compact three-manifold arises as the Cauchy hypersurface of a globally hyperbolic Lorentzian four-manifold equipped with a skew-torsion parallel spinor. Building on these results, we study the interaction between the four-dimensional Neveu-Schwarz supergravity evolution flow on an abelian bundle gerbe and the spinorial evolution flow determined by its supersymmetric conditions, which we prove to be well-posed and compatible. This establishes the well-posedness of the supersymmetric Neveu-Schwarz system in four dimensions and provides an initial-data characterization of supersymmetry. Furthermore, we obtain a strong rigidity result stating that every globally hyperbolic supersymmetric Neveu-Schwarz solution with a compact Cauchy hypersurface is flat and has vanishing bundle-gerbe curvature.

titles.title: The Cauchy problem for skew-torsion-parallel spinors with applications to supergravity

abstracts.value: Velocity gradients compatible with rotation have been reported across certain nearby cosmic filaments. We show that rotational momentum might be generated in filaments in the local Universe in the presence of a cosmological constant (local dark energy) based on the theorem stating the general function for the equivalence of the gravitational field of a sphere and that of a point mass. We investigated how the cosmological constant modifies the finite-time acquisition and retention of angular momentum in an open filamentary core. Although its isotropic force exerts no direct axial torque, rotational motion can be seeded by tidal interactions with surrounding matter and incoming streams. Early tidal torques establish an imbalance in axial angular momentum, while the subsequent orbit crossing amplifies the resulting rotation, and ultimately, the cosmological constant is able to modify tidal-mode growth and finite-time angular momentum delivery.

abstracts.value: The quantum switch applies two operations in a coherent superposition of their causal orders and is a simple example of indefinite causal order. No quantum circuit that uses each operation once in a definite order can even describe it, yet photonic experiments have demonstrated its physical realization. We ask how many calls to the black-box operations a quantum computer in the circuit model needs to reproduce the switch. If one of the black boxes is known to be unitary, three calls suffice. For general channels on a $d$-dimensional system, we prove three results. In all three, circuits may use classical feed-forward and unlimited ancillary quantum memory. First, no finite number of calls suffices for exact simulation in the worst case. Second, approximation to any fixed error below $1/2$, measured in half the diamond norm, requires $Ω(d^{1/4})$ calls, exponential in the number of qubits. Third, an ordinary circuit can require exponentially many calls to obtain a single bit that the switch extracts with a few uses. We consider a device whose actual noise is dephasing in a fixed unknown basis and test it against a theoretical depolarizing model. The two channels have the same entanglement and average gate fidelities, so these figures alone do not distinguish them. At fixed noise strength, the quantum switch tells them apart with a number of device uses independent of $d$, whereas the circuit model requires $Ω(d^{1/16})$ calls. Noise characterization is needed for quantum error correction, and this gives a provable query advantage of the switch in a task relevant to practical quantum computing. We invite future work that extends such advantages to more practical computing tasks.

titles.title: Infinite or indefinite: the query cost of simulating the quantum switch

abstracts.value: The Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) has observed the northern sky observable from Palomar Observatory since March 2018, accumulating a median of a thousand photometric measurements across $gri$ for each of more than a billion sources. We describe the initial data release (DR1) of the ZTF Variability Archive (ZVAR) which provides image difference forced photometry, candidate periods, and variability metrics for approximately 1.3 billion sources in ZTF having an identification in Pan-STARRS1 DR1 (PS1). The data cover the 5.37 year interval between March 2018 and July 2023. ZVAR is sensitive to periods between 5 minutes and 2.7 years. We also describe tools for accessing the ZVAR data.

abstracts.value: We develop a symmetry-based approach to renormalization for even-dimensional Einstein-AdS gravity based on infinitesimal bulk Weyl transformations that preserve its field equations asymptotically. We determine a bulk-covariant completion of the Einstein-Hilbert density by requiring its variation under restricted Weyl transformations with parameter $Σ(X)$ to vanish modulo terms whose integrals remain finite as the radial cutoff is removed. This requirement induces two types of compensating terms with fixed couplings: the Euler density and a hierarchy of covariant total derivatives. The resulting recursive relations admit a factorized solution in terms of shifted Laplacians, yielding a closed-form completion in arbitrary even bulk dimensions. On Einstein backgrounds, these expressions agree, after matching normalizations, with those obtained through the ambient construction of conformal invariants. The associated renormalized-volume identity establishes on-shell finiteness for Euclidean AlAdS Einstein geometries in arbitrary even dimensions. The prescription reproduces the known conformally renormalized actions in four, six and eight dimensions and provides an explicit ten-dimensional completion involving powers of the Laplacian up to $\Box^3$. Applications to eight- and ten-dimensional AdS black holes with non-conformally-flat Einstein horizons yield finite on-shell actions in agreement with Holographic Renormalization.

titles.title: Holographic Counterterms from Restricted Weyl Symmetry in Even-Dimensional Einstein-AdS Gravity

abstracts.value: In a neutron star low-mass X-ray binary, heavy elements (with mass number ~100) are believed to be synthesized through the rapid-proton (rp) capture process, as indirectly indicated by the long tail of X-ray burst light curves. Although direct evidence for the rp-process was lacking so far, we reported in our previous study that an unidentified hump is present at ~30 keV of the Suzaku spectra of Aquila X-1 in its hard state. The feature was tentatively identified with a recombination quasi-continuum from highly ionized ions of cadmium or indium, which are possibly produced by the rp process during X-ray bursts and lifted up into the neutron-star atmosphere. To reinforce this scenario, we quantitatively evaluated the physical conditions of the assumed emitting region in the atmosphere, and confirmed that the scenario is possible when the putative rp-process ashes in the atmosphere has ~10^7 times higher abundances than their solar values. The results are compared with theoretical model calculations for the nucleosynthesis in X-ray bursts. We suggest that the observed spectral hump is a radiative recombination feature from the stable isotope 106Cd, produced in X-ray bursts via the rp-process. Further issues about the detectability are briefly discussed.
