abstracts.value: The natal kicks imparted to neutron stars and black holes at birth are critical for understanding massive-star evolution, compact-object formation, and compact binary merger rates. However, constraining these kicks is challenging, since they cannot be directly observed. Here, we outline a framework for inferring natal kick probability distributions for compact binaries. Our method embeds the rapid binary-population code COSMIC in a Monte-Carlo workflow that evolves ensembles of simulated binaries. From those which host compact objects, we can select subsets that match the observational characteristics of any given system (e.g. component masses, orbital period, mass-transfer status, systemic velocity). As a proof-of-concept, we apply this framework to six compact binaries spanning a wide range of companion masses and compact-object types. For each system, we identify the evolutionary channel(s) that could have led to the current observational characteristics, and isolate regions of allowed natal kicks and progenitor parameter space. We reconfirm that at least one black hole system, XTE J1118+480, must have received a natal kick $v_{\rm NK} > 100$ km s$^{-1}$. The neutron-star system, GX 301-2, is also inferred to have received an impulsive kick exceeding 280 km s$^{-1}$. We discuss the strengths and limitations associated with population-synthesis-based inference methods and explore the effects of adopting different prescriptions for critical binary evolution phases. We provide a detailed demonstration of the non-linear relationship between $v_{\rm NK}$ and $v_{\rm sys}$, highlighting the shortcomings of relying on observations alone to measure natal kicks. The inferred kick velocity distributions across our benchmark sample are generally consistent with previous constraints.

titles.title: Natal Kicks of Compact Binaries: I. Population Synthesis Framework and Illustrative Examples

abstracts.value: We show that Grover's algorithm can be used to parametrically accelerate wave-like dark matter searches. Despite having a finite coherence time $τ$, wavelike dark matter can imprint a coherent $O(1)$ phase onto a sensor through a dispersive coupling over an integration time which significantly exceeds $τ$. As such, we show that dark matter can be used as a repeatable quantum phase gate in a quantum device. If the sensor is prepared in a superposition of frequencies, we show that this phase can be transferred to a qubit register and digitized. The qubits are thus available for quantum computational processing in which dark matter can take part as a coherent gate. We show that Grover's algorithm can be used to speed up a search for dark matter in $N_{\rm bins}$ frequency bins by a factor of $\sqrt{N_{\rm bins}}$. Although the technological challenges to implementing such a search remain substantial, this demonstrates that there is no fundamental obstruction to accelerating wave-like dark matter searches with quantum computational techniques over many coherence times.

titles.title: A Grover-Accelerated Search for Dark Matter

abstracts.value: Einstein gravity, with a few exceptions, only admits nonlocal observables. This feature is often attributed to diffeomorphism invariance, since a gravitational field can thereby locally be transformed away. We show this attribution to be incorrect by constructing infinitely many exact ultralocal Dirac observables in (velocity dominated aka electric) Carroll gravity. The latter describes Einstein gravity's ultrarelativistic limit, is fully diffeomorphism invariant, and of independent interest in a variety of contexts. Starting from these Carroll observables a systematic construction of Dirac observables for Einstein gravity is outlined. The resulting "post-Carrollian" expansion is organized by the number of spatial gradients or fractional inverse powers of Newton's constant, where each partial sum is local.

titles.title: Gravitational observables from a post-Carrollian expansion

abstracts.value: Neutrino flavor measurements test physics beyond the Standard Model that modifies neutrino production, propagation, or detection. IceCube has measured the flavor composition of the astrophysical neutrino flux up to PeV energies. Next-generation experiments will extend flavor measurements to the ultra-high-energy (UHE) regime, $100\,\mathrm{PeV}$-$10\,\mathrm{EeV}$, by combining in-ice radio detection with Earth-skimming tau neutrinos. We present the first study of the new-physics reach of these projected UHE flavor measurements. We take Lorentz invariance violation (LIV) as a benchmark, since its effects grow as a power of the neutrino energy. We find that UHE flavor ratios will be the most sensitive probe of LIV for operators of dimension four and higher, improving on current bounds from all sectors by up to twenty orders of magnitude. Three-flavor observables improve this sensitivity by up to an order of magnitude over Earth-skimming tau neutrinos alone.

titles.title: New Physics in Ultra-High-Energy Neutrino Flavor

abstracts.value: It is well-known that in the merger of a black-hole binary with spins aligned with the orbital angular momentum, the spin of the final black hole always increases with the spin of the components. We show that this very intuitive behavior is violated in black hole--neutron star binaries, where the spin of the final black hole actually decreases as the spin of the neutron star increases. Using a large set of binaries with different spins and mass ratios, we identify the mechanism behind this surprising result in the nonlinear dynamics of the tidal disruption, which drives a substantial loss of angular momentum via dynamical ejecta, in some cases comparable to that radiated via gravitational waves. Our results highlight that the spin evolution of stellar-mass black holes involved in binary mergers is different from what normally assumed, far more complex, and interesting.

titles.title: Spins do not add: why rotating stars do not help spin-up black holes in binaries

abstracts.value: Krylov complexity has become a central probe of operator growth, scrambling, and quantum chaos. Yet, a basic fact hinders its experimental study: laboratory quantum systems are routinely driven in time, whereas the Krylov construction assumes a fixed generator and breaks down once the Hamiltonian varies. Here, we solve the time-dependent many-body Krylov problem exactly and in closed form for scale- and rotation-invariant systems realized in current quantum-simulation and control platforms. We find exact relations that map the driven dynamics onto mutually orthogonal Krylov subspaces and yield a closed-form spread complexity, determined solely by the spectral properties of the initial Hamiltonian and the driving schedule. The construction extends to Liouville space and solves the time-dependent density-matrix Krylov problem, which makes the Krylov dynamics of initial thermal states experimentally accessible. In scale-invariant quantum gases, such as the driven Lieb-Liniger model, the Tonks-Girardeau gas, and the Calogero-Sutherland model, the complexity is set by the width of the atomic cloud and its rate of change, directly accessible via in situ and time-of-flight imaging. In rotation-invariant spin systems such as the Haldane-Shastry and central-spin models, it is governed by collective spin precession that can be probed and read out in trapped-ion, cavity-QED, and circuit-QED platforms.

titles.title: Probing Krylov Dynamics in Driven Many-Body Systems

abstracts.value: Neutrinos may experience a new long-range force that distinguishes their flavors, mediated by an ultralight neutral boson of a new $U(1)'$ gauge symmetry and sourced by the electrons and nucleons of ordinary matter. Atmospheric neutrinos that cross the Earth would then feel a flavor-dependent potential that alters their oscillations. When the range of the force is about one Earth radius or less, this potential varies from point to point along each neutrino's path, since it comes mostly from the matter near the neutrino. Earlier limits approximated it, either as constant along the path or as following the local density of matter. We compute it exactly at every point of each path, for the Earth model of the IceCube analysis and over the distribution of heights at which the neutrinos are produced, and use it to analyze the 8-yr public IceCube DeepCore sample with the systematic uncertainties of that analysis. For mediator masses from $10^{-15}$ to $10^{-9}$ eV, where the Earth alone sources the potential, we set upper limits at 90% confidence level on the coupling of eight of 14 $U(1)'$ symmetries, those whose potential differs between $ν_μ$ and $ν_τ$. A potential held at its value at the detector would weaken our limits by factors of about 1-3. Below about $10^{-11}$-$10^{-10}$ eV, depending on the symmetry, our limits are stronger than those from tests of the equivalence principle.

titles.title: Earth-sized tests of long-range neutrino interactions

abstracts.value: We construct a calibrated model of the proton generalized transverse-momentum-dependent distribution (GTMD) $F_{1,1}$ in the real, staple-even valence-$u$ sector at zero skewness. Experimental measurements, lattice matrix elements, and phenomenological distributions enter through a single shared light-front state, organized as a symmetry-resolved tree tensor network in which color-singlet structure, exchange statistics, and the additive $J_z$ and $I_z$ charges are built in. Classical and quantum geometric nodes represent the residual transverse response. The GTMD is defined with soft subtraction, one-loop nonsinglet matching, NLO collinear evolution, and an explicit nonperturbative joint closure, so that each input is used with its own operator convention and scale. Calibrating against correlated ART25 transverse projections, HERA inclusive data, and lattice, elastic, and static information gives a simple picture. The forward inputs narrow the attainable transverse response by about $81\%$ at $x=0.4$. The simultaneous dependence on quark momentum and momentum transfer, however, is untouched by any of them: a deformation that leaves every present input invariant moves the nonforward value from $0.588$ to $0.378\,\mathrm{GeV}^{-2}$. Dense momentum-space surfaces and finite-transfer-window phase-space maps show the structure this freedom controls. The tensor-network organization is chosen with composition in mind. The same shared subunits, operator hierarchy, and qualification protocol extend to the neutron, the spin-1 deuteron, and spin-$3/2$ nuclei, where the number of symmetry and exchange constraints grows quickly and a structural representation becomes the practical route. The quantum circuits are verified feature maps and state encodings; their capacity and cost are measured alongside the classical blocks.

abstracts.value: Superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors (SNSPDs) can be made sensitive to single photons with near-unity detection efficiency, ultra-low dark-count rates, and sub-nanosecond timing jitter over a broad wavelength range. However, many studies report data inconsistently, often emphasizing a single performance metric without considering overall device performance. This inconsistent data reporting limits the field, as it makes it difficult to determine which device characteristics are most important. Different applications require functionalities that may conflict with one another; for example, longer-wavelength operation may require lower operating temperatures. Moreover, there is no universally accepted metric for defining the figures of merit of an SNSPD. In this work, we amass a dataset representing the state of the art of SNSPD fabrication, including operating temperature, operating wavelength, photon count rates (PCR), and dark count rates (DCR). We fit the PCR curves and suggest using the saturation plateau length to gauge the SNSPD's sensitivity. We then fit the DCR and compare the PCR and DCR. Using this approach, we establish a quantitative framework to determine the optimal biasing condition for a given device and to determine the device's sensitivity at that optimal biasing condition, enabling meaningful comparisons across disparate devices. Additionally, we offer concrete benchmarks for measuring device performance.

titles.title: Establishing Standards for Assessment and Reporting of SNSPD Performance

abstracts.value: We investigate quantum gate teleportation as a primitive for satellite-enabled distributed quantum computing. In the considered architecture, a satellite distributes entangled photon pairs to two optical ground stations, which transfer the shared quantum resource to remote quantum processing units. This entanglement is then used to implement a nonlocal controlled-NOT gate between two circuit qubits located in different processors. We formulate the minimal four-qubit protocol, consisting of two network qubits that provide the entangled resource and two circuit qubits on which the distributed gate is performed. Atmospheric propagation effects in the gravitational field are modeled through an effective two-qubit depolarizing channel whose parameters depend on atmospheric and optical quantities, including the Fried parameter and receiver aperture. The performance of the protocol is quantified by the fidelity between the ideal CNOT output state and the state produced by noisy quantum gate teleportation. Our results show that the fidelity is governed by the quality of the distributed entanglement and depends jointly on atmospheric coherence, aperture size, and effective depolarization strength. These findings connect physical-layer modeling of satellite optical channels with gate-level performance in distributed quantum computing.

titles.title: Towards Distributed Quantum Computing: Quantum Gate Teleportation via Satellite-Distributed Entanglement under Atmospheric Depolarization

abstracts.value: Gas-rich ultra-diffuse galaxies (UDGs) provide powerful tests of galaxy formation models at low surface densities. However, the structure of their neutral atomic hydrogen (HI) remains poorly constrained, hampering our understanding of this population. We present FRIDA (Finding Rotation In ultra-Diffuse gAlaxies), a MeerKAT and VLA programme providing high-resolution HI data of 12 gas-rich UDGs. In this paper, we introduce our sample and delve into the associated observations and data reduction. We derive HI fluxes, masses ($M_{\rm HI}$), and resolved surface density profiles ($Σ_{\rm HI}(R)$). We find extended ($\sim 7-30\ \rm{kpc}$ in radius) and regular HI emission in our UDGs, and we report the discovery of a satellite around one of them. Most UDGs in FRIDA have $Σ_{\rm HI}(R)$ profiles with flat inner parts reaching $Σ_{\rm HI}(R)\approx 4\ M_\odot\ \rm{pc^{-2}}$ near their centres, which then decline exponentially in their outer parts. By modelling the HI morphology of the UDGs, we find a median inclination of $43^\circ$, in agreement with theoretical expectations for disc galaxies under UDG selection effects. Moreover, we place our UDGs in the $M_{\rm HI}-R_{\rm HI}$ and $M_{\rm HI}-R_{\rm 50,HI}$ mass-size relations, where $R_{\rm HI}$ is radius at which $Σ_{\rm HI}(R)=1\ M_\odot \rm{pc^{-2}}$, and $R_{\rm 50,HI}$ is the radius enclosing $50\%$ of $M_{\rm HI}$. While our UDGs lie within the scatter of the relations, they systematically fall on their upper side, being slightly (by $\sim 15-25\%$) more extended and of lower mean $Σ_{\rm HI}$ (by $\sim 25-35\%$) than average galaxies at similar $M_{\rm HI}$. Moreover, we find that $Σ_{\rm HI}(R/R_{\rm HI})$ and $M_{\rm HI}(<R)/M_{\rm HI}$ for UDGs follow an intermediate trend between late-type discs and early-type galaxies, with a large overlap with Sa galaxies.

titles.title: FRIDA: Finding Rotation In ultra-Diffuse gAlaxies. I. Programme overview, resolved gas density profiles, and HI mass-size relation

abstracts.value: How much memory does a quantum device need to prepare systems one at a time? We address this question through the lens of quantum resource theories, which formalize physical restrictions on how the memory may interact with the stream of systems it processes. By comparing sequential with collective preparation, we show that under general assumptions both have the same asymptotic memory cost per output. Still, sequential preparation can require an unboundedly larger memory than collective one, and we investigate how this gap depends on the physical restrictions on the allowed interactions. For energy-conserving unitaries, we determine both optimal memory dimensions needed for preparing pure states from an energy eigenstate, and find that the extra memory required sequentially either remains bounded or grows logarithmically with the number of outputs. Under noisy operations, we reveal transformations for which one auxiliary qubit suffices for preparing arbitrarily many independent outputs collectively, while no memory of fixed dimension can deliver them sequentially. Finally, for sequential protocols that repeat a fixed interaction, we show that a $d$-dimensional memory that succeeds for $d^2$ rounds will succeed forever, and that such a sequential preparation is equivalent to quantum catalysis.

titles.title: The memory cost of sequential quantum state preparation

abstracts.value: Precise measurements of the baryonic acoustic oscillation (BAO) peak position are one of the key goals in modern galaxy surveys. We investigate the impact of the monopole fluctuations in galaxy surveys on the BAO peak position in the galaxy two-point redshift-space multipole-correlation functions. The background mean density of a galaxy sample is estimated from the survey itself by averaging the observed galaxy number density, and this averaged number density (monopole) is subtracted to obtain the observed galaxy number density fluctuation, which includes an additional contribution from the monopole fluctuations, propagating to galaxy clustering analysis. We compute the contributions of the monopole fluctuations to the redshift-space multipole-correlation functions. While the monopole contributions in galaxy two-point correlation function are anisotropic and non-negligible in amplitude, the contributions are so smooth around the BAO peak position that they are almost completely absorbed in the BAO broadband model, leaving the BAO peak position unaffected at the sub-percent level. Our results demonstrate the robustness of the BAO analysis against the unknown systematic error.

titles.title: Robustness of the Baryonic Acoustic Oscillation Peak Position against Monopole Fluctuations in Galaxy Surveys

abstracts.value: We derived a geometrical distance of the black-hole X-ray binary 4U 1543-475 based on X-ray dust-scattering rings associated with its 1992 and 2002 outbursts. We analyzed archival ROSAT and XMM-Newton observations and identified an X-ray dust-scattering ring in each observation, produced by two different dust layers along the line of sight. By combining the angular radii of the rings with the independently determined distances of the scattering dust layers and the epochs of the corresponding outbursts, we derive a best-constrained distance to 4U 1543-475 of 4.6 $\pm$ 0.2 kpc. This value is substantially smaller than the distance of 7.5 kpc commonly adopted in the literature and has important implications for the inferred physical properties of the system. In particular, the revised distance favors the presence of a low-mass extended-horizontal-branch donor star over a main-sequence star, calling for a reassessment of the dynamical parameters of the binary and, consequently, of the black-hole mass. The smaller distance also affects the inferred properties of the relativistic jet and the estimate of black-hole spin derived from the spectral continuum-fitting.

abstracts.value: We present the largest uniform study to date of 50 thermonuclear Type Ia supernovae interacting with circumstellar medium (SNe Ia-CSM). As the first paper in a series delineating the population properties of this class, this work focuses specifically on a uniform analysis of their light curves. Our results show that SNe Ia-CSM display a significantly more uniform light-curve morphology than interacting core-collapse SNe IIn, closely resembling the luminous-slow subgroup. The Ia-CSM sample spans approximately an order of magnitude in peak luminosity, total timescale, and radiated energy, with a median optical peak luminosity of $\approx2\times10^{43}$ erg s$^{-1}$ ($\approx-20$ mag). We find a distinct bimodality in the radiated energy distribution: a predominant population of energetic events with $\approx 2\times10^{50}$ erg and characteristic timescales of $\approx100$ days, and a secondary population that is roughly an order of magnitude less energetic with shorter timescales of $\approx50$ days. Decomposition of the luminosity contributions from underlying SN Ia and CSM interaction by the Ia-CSM spectral classification reveals a diverse range of underlying SN Ia subtypes spanning from luminous 1991T-like to faint 1991bg-like. Both SN Ia and CSM properties are broadly consistent with the core-degenerate channel resulting from common-envelope evolution followed by core merger, where the presence of dense CSM is dictated by the delay time between the common-envelope phase and the thermonuclear explosion. Subsequent papers in this series will utilize numerical simulations, semi-analytical modeling, spectroscopy, and host-galaxy environments to further constrain the progenitor and explosion pathways to SNe Ia-CSM.

abstracts.value: Weak probes can record whether neighboring spins are aligned without revealing their common orientation. Reading the probes can then herald a projection of an unknown spin state onto the aligned subspace that preserves every coherence within it. We ask how often this projection succeeds when the probes are read separately or jointly. For binary pure product records and zero false positives, we derive the exact optimum over all separable measurements, and hence over all local operations and classical communication. It is the probability that one-sided local witnesses exclude every alternative, and simultaneous local measurements attain it. Joint readout can do better by accepting coherent combinations of ambiguous outcomes in which the alternatives cancel. For pairwise parity records on a connected simple graph, it beats every local strategy exactly when the graph has a loop, at all record overlaps strictly between zero and one. For general binary linear records, the condition is an irreducible dependency among at least three records. The advantage lowers the leading power of the efficiency at weak recording. On a triangle the efficiency becomes linear rather than quadratic in the witness probability, and a three-pulse coherent-light receiver captures this gain with a single click. Extensions treat targets spanning several patterns and a noisy comparison at a common output fidelity.

titles.title: Faithful filtering of constrained quantum records: Local limits and collective advantage from loops

abstracts.value: We develop a self-consistent relativistic second random-phase approximation (RSRPA) based on covariant energy density functional with density dependent point-coupling interaction. The formalism extends the conventional simple configuration space composed of particle-hole ($p$-$h$) transitions by including two-particle-two-hole ($2p$-$2h$) configurations through a generalized Thouless ansatz and a time-dependent variational principle. To ensure consistency with the underlying mean-field ground state and avoid the double counting of correlations, we implement the subtraction method, in which the static contribution is removed from the residual interaction. The first applications of the RSRPA include studies of isoscalar and isovector giant monopole (ISGMR and IVGMR) and quadrupole resonances (ISGQR and IVGQR) in $^{16}$O, which demonstrate the importance of $2p$-$2h$ couplings to describe the fragmentation of the transition strength and the stabilizing role of the subtraction method.

abstracts.value: We propose an effective framework relating correlation geometry to stochastic flows of correlation projectors. Physical configurations are encoded by measures on spaces of self-adjoint operators, with physical equivalence defined by unitary conjugation. Assuming a smooth, spectrally separated correlation sector, local orthonormal frames define a Wilczek--Zee connection, while a Stratonovich gradient-flow ansatz preserves the projector constraints. In a local continuum approximation with massive fast modes, standard one-loop methods generate Yang--Mills-type terms and curvature terms of Einstein--Hilbert form. Along a smooth closed path, the trace of a cyclic product of projectors converges to the trace of the parallel-transport operator as the discretization is refined. We examine possible geometric, disordered, and topological regimes and motivate the stochastic dynamics through an effective open-system description. The first-order frame action defines a symplectic structure on the projector sector, providing a starting point for its relation to gravitational canonical variables. We identify the matching conditions required for an Ashtekar phase-space description and the assumptions connecting correlation geometry to induced interactions and emergent spacetime.

titles.title: Correlation Geometry and Emergent Space-Time from Stochastic Correlation Flows

abstracts.value: Natal kicks - kinematic impulses to neutron stars and black holes at birth - play a decisive role in the end-stage evolution of binaries hosting massive stars, in determining the global phase-space properties of compact objects, and in setting expected merger-rates detectable through gravitational-wave observations. Inferring the kick ($v_{\rm NK}$) for individual systems requires well constrained binary system properties and centre-of-mass kinematics, which must then be modelled to constrain likely system characteristics at supernova. As a result, population-wide studies of kicks remain few and far between. Here, we model plausible evolutionary histories for 68 accreting binaries, encompassing almost all black-hole and neutron-star X-ray binaries with 3D kinematics measurements, constraining allowed $v_{\rm NK}$ distributions for each source using a simulation framework presented in our previous paper. The resultant $v_{\rm NK}$ distribution for the sample can be simply represented by a broad Gamma distribution with mean $v_{\rm NK}$ = $128^{+17}_{-15}$ km s$^{-1}$ and scatter $σ$ = 117 km s$^{-1}$. Intriguingly, the distributions for black-hole vs. neutron-star systems are found to be formally indistinguishable. Despite still being limited by small-number statistics, we find that black holes can receive large natal kicks, and that kicks for all remnant types span similar ranges (0-700 km s$^{-1}$). There is a hint, but no statistically significant evidence at present, for $v_{\rm NK}$ scaling inversely with black-hole mass. Our work suggests either that similar physics drives kicks and shows evidence for effects beyond simplistic fallback-moderated scaling for black holes, or that selection effects conspire to erase differences between remnant types in current accreting-binary samples. Larger samples are needed to provide robust discriminatory tests between these possibilities.

titles.title: Natal Kicks of Compact Binaries: II. Neutron-star and black-hole systems share similar kick distributions

abstracts.value: Single-crystal diamond is the reference solid-state technology for fast neutron detection in fusion devices. Despite this, its complex manufacturing increases their costs and puts limitations on their geometry. Moreover, the limits in their long-term stability and their behaviour in harsh environments further constraint its applications. Synthetic sapphire (Al2O2) is a promising alternative as a solid state detector material: it is available in large, low-cost wafers and features both a wider bandgap and a higher displacement energy compared to diamond. Despite this, it has so far received little-to-no attention as a neutron detector. This work presents the first steps of a development programme for sapphire-based fast neutron detectors. Eight prototypes with 4.5 x 4.5 mm2 and 9 x 9 mm2 active areas and 625 um thickness were fabricated from commercial wafers with Al-Si electrodes and coupled to different electronic configurations. All prototypes detected 5.47 MeV alpha particles from a 241Am source, confirming the viability of both the fabrication process and the use of sapphire as an active material. The small signals (30-40 mV over a peak-to-peak noise of about 8 mV) and the count rate increasing with bias indicate that sapphires will require higher electric fields than the ones experimented in the work (up to about 2.5 kV). Geant4 simulations were also used to estimate the response of a sapphire detector to 14.06 MeV (DT) neutrons, highlighting the perspectives of the detector as a fusion diagnostic.

abstracts.value: CosmoSim is an open-source tool for simulating gravitational lenses and reconstructing lens mass distributions, either by ray tracing a parametric lens model or through a Roulette expansion of the lens potential. It is also used to generate the large, labelled synthetic image sets needed to train machine-learning (ML) parameter estimators. We present the first application of CosmoSim to real data. A convolutional neural network trained only on CosmoSim images estimates Singular Isothermal Ellipsoid lens and source parameters directly from observed images. We test the pipeline on 21 images of 19 strong lenses from Euclid and the AGEL survey, after removing the foreground lens light with a custom decontamination tool built on AstroPy. As a case study we reconstruct the Einstein Cross NGC 6505 both from the lens model published by the discovery team and from parameters predicted by our ML model. Both reconstructions recover the observed four-image structure, and the ML-based reconstruction performs at least as well as the literature-based one: it scores better on masked structural similarity, intersection-over-union and Chamfer distance, with an essentially equal Hausdorff distance. Across the ensemble, the predicted Einstein radii are consistent with catalogued values within the quoted uncertainties (mean relative difference 0.08 for Euclid and 0.19 for AGEL lenses), and the enclosed masses agree to within a median of 0.12 dex. The predicted ellipticities differ systematically from the catalogued values, while the comparison of orientations is inconclusive. These results establish CosmoSim as a tool that can be applied directly to observational data.

titles.title: CosmoSim: Lens-parameter estimation of the Einstein Cross NGC 6505 using machine learning

abstracts.value: We develop a gauge-independent theory of magnetic reconnection beyond the standard special-relativistic framework of inertial systems in flat spacetime. Our definitions of reconnection and its rate are independent of reference frame and coordinate system, allowing physical effects of gravity and net linear acceleration to be distinguished from coordinate effects. We extend the mesoscale theory of Liu et al. [PRL 118, 085101 (2017)], in which the reconnection rate depends on physics both within the diffusion region and in an upstream ideal, force-free region. The theory identifies three non-inertial and curved-spacetime (NICS) effects, including gravitationally induced magnetic tension: gravitational distortion of the reconnection plane changes the curvature of magnetic field lines. Applying the theory to a simplified accretion plasma near )a compact object, we find that (1) whether gravity increases or decreases the reconnection rate depends on the system's orientation relative to the gravitational source, with the greatest increase occurring when the outflow jet points toward or away from the source; and (2) the magnitude of the gravitational effect scales with the dimensionless parameter $\barκ \equiv r_sΔy^2/r^3$, where $r$ is the Schwarzschild radial coordinate, $r_s$ is the source's Schwarzschild radius, and $Δy$ is the mesoscale length.

titles.title: General Relativistic and Non-Inertial Effects on Magnetic Reconnection Rates

abstracts.value: Standard Bell inequalities rely on measurement independence, the assumption that measurement settings are perfectly decoupled from the source of correlations. We demonstrate that embedding Bell scenarios into larger causal networks naturally overcomes this limitation. This embedding yields experimentally accessible lower and upper bounds on measurement dependence, the incompatibility of which certifies nonclassicality directly from data, without assuming a priori freedom of choice. We formulate a general linear-programming framework to systematically derive these measurement-dependence consistency (MDC) Bell inequalities. By bypassing standard non-convexity hurdles, this approach significantly outperforms existing techniques in computational simplicity and noise robustness. Finally, we reveal that genuine quantum nonlocality can be certified even for correlations exceeding the Tsirelson bound, and demonstrate our method's broad applicability to multi-outcome and multipartite Bell tests.

titles.title: Bounding Freedom of Choice via Causal Network Embeddings

abstracts.value: We revisit the regularized on-shell actions of rotating electrically charged AdS black holes of gauged supergravity via holographic renormalization and background subtraction, with a particular emphasis on the frame in which the radial cutoff is placed. For holographic renormalization, the asymptotically global AdS frame, recently employed in seven dimensions, works equally well in five and six dimensions: the renormalized on-shell action of the AdS$_d$ black holes with $S^1\times S^{d-2}$ conformal boundaries satisfies the quantum statistical relation, up to a parameter-independent Casimir term in odd dimensions, and thereby places the holographic comparisons that so far relied on this relation on a first-principles footing. Background subtraction, in contrast, fails to reproduce this result in the same frame; the mismatch, which we identify exactly in terms of the Casimir term and the counterterms, demands a criterion for the cutoff surface yet to be established. For precision holography, our results settle the choice of frame for holographic renormalization with conformally flat boundaries and delineate the ambiguities that remain in background subtraction and in holographic renormalization for boundaries that are not conformally flat.

titles.title: Anatomy of AdS black hole on-shell actions

abstracts.value: Accurate calibration of the detector response is essential for precision gravitational-wave (GW) observations. In the Back-linked Fabry-Perot Interferometer (BLFPI), which employs Fabry-Perot cavities to achieve high GW sensitivity, accurate calibration of the cavity response is particularly important because residual calibration errors directly limit the suppression of laser frequency noise. However, no practical calibration strategy for the cavity response has yet been established. In this paper, we propose a method for calibrating the cavity response using a null channel constructed from the three interferometer outputs of the triangular laser-link configuration. In null channel, GW signals are canceled and residual laser frequency noise indicates errors in the cavity response estimates. Therefore we can estimate the cavity response by optimizing the response parameters to minimize the integrated power of the null channel. We derive the estimation bias introduced by technical noise analytically and evaluate the performance of the proposed method numerically. The results show that the residual laser frequency noise after calibration is more than an order of magnitude below the designed BLFPI sensitivity throughout the observation band. This demonstrates that the proposed null-channel calibration method achieves the accuracy required for effective subtraction of laser frequency noise.

titles.title: Accurate calibration method of the Back-linked Fabry Perot interferometer using null channel for space-based gravitational wave antenna

abstracts.value: The spatial distribution of cluster-lensed star transients with respect to the macroscopic critical curve (CC) is sensitive to underlying substructures predicted by different classes of dark matter (DM) models. \citet{Broadhurst_2025} have shown that wave-like DM composed of ultra-light bosons better explains both the width and negative skewness (towards the interior of the CC) of the lensed star spatial distribution discovered in the ``Dragon'' lensed galaxy ($z = 0.73$) in the Abell 370 (A370, $z = 0.375$) cluster field, compared with the case of regular cold dark matter (CDM) subhaloes. In this work, we consider the case of self-interacting DM (SIDM) and investigate how the lensed star spatial distribution depends on the velocity-dependent self-interaction cross-section of SIDM particles, and whether constraints can be placed on the cross-section strength at relevant velocities. Establishing a cross-section strength-dependent (sub)halo gravothermal core-collapse probability, we found that the SIDM appears to be the only known class of models thus far in which the sign of skewness is set by its own particle parameters. The observed lensed star distribution in the Dragon galaxy can be well explained, in terms of both skewness and width, when a significant fraction of subhaloes have undergone core collapse and exhibit a steep power-law density slope. Given the cluster redshift, this qualitatively favours an (effective) cross-section strength of $500 -1000\,\textrm{cm}^{2}/\textrm{g}$ for halos with mass $10^{6} - 10^{8}\,M_{\odot}$ (velocity dispersion of $\sim 1-10\,\rm{km}/\rm{s}$), when the role of environmental effects on the core-collapse (de)acceleration is not considered, and limits the three-dimensional inner density slope of the collapsed halo to $Γ\gtrsim 2.5$ (Bayes factor of $\sim 10^{2}$).

titles.title: Self-interacting Dark Matter signatures from stars extremely magnified by galaxy clusters

abstracts.value: Current and future spectroscopic and photometric galaxy surveys will deliver unprecedented numbers of galaxies, with expected counts in the tens of millions. To answer the computational challenges posed by these surveys, in this paper we present VIDE 2.0, a significantly improved and enhanced void finding algorithm and analysis pipeline based on VIDE. Leveraging the parameter-free identification of voids via a Voronoi tessellation and watershed scheme, we implement a robust mechanism for handling survey boundaries and incompleteness without relying on vast numbers of boundary particles. This new method identifies edge galaxies and flags voids contaminated by their presence. The mechanism is fully deterministic, producing bit-for-bit reproducible catalogs from identical inputs. An automatic rule for setting the mask resolution renders the entire pipeline parameter-free. Combined with other performance enhancements to the underlying VIDE engine, we find significant ($>100\times$) speedups and a dramatic reduction in memory usage compared to previous versions: a 12-million-galaxy DESI Y1-class mock catalog now completes in roughly 15 minutes on a single laptop, where VIDE 1.0 could not run a catalog of even $10^6$ galaxies on the same hardware. We are also able to identify voids existing closer to survey boundaries via deterministic per-void contamination flags, maximizing their statistical potential. We exercise the upgraded pipeline on two large mock suites (MultiDark-Patchy DR12 and AbacusSummit DESI Y1 ELG), demonstrating converged cosmic-variance covariances for the void number function, the void-galaxy cross-correlation, and the void ellipticity distribution -- key ingredients for Stage IV void cosmology. VIDE 2.0 is now well suited to handle large numbers of galaxies in mock and real observations, and ready to tackle the challenges of future campaigns.

titles.title: VIDE 2.0: Robust, Scalable Void Finding for Extremely Large Galaxy Surveys

abstracts.value: In this paper, we construct new self-gravitating solutions for the four-dimensional $SU(2)$ Einstein non-linear sigma model and the Einstein-Skyrme model, both minimally coupled to the Maxwell field, which describes spinning pulsed mesonic tubes. These solutions are gyratonic in the sense that they are characterized by a propagation axis and possess angular momentum. The gyratonic solutions are described by a smooth matter distribution, which is free of curvature singularities. The maximum of the energy density is concentrated on a tube around the propagation axis. We first consider the $SU(2)$ non-linear sigma model minimally coupled to General Relativity and the Maxwell field, constructing asymptotically flat, spinning, pulsed gyratonic solutions. Subsequently, we include the Skyrme term in the analysis. In this case, we show that in order to maintain the resolvability of the matter field equations, the spacetime must be asymptotically de Sitter. It is also shown that, despite the fact that the total topological charge is zero, these solutions possess a non-zero topological charge density.

titles.title: Self-gravitating spinning mesonic tubes

abstracts.value: In recent years, rapid advancements in semiconductor manufacturing have underscored the critical need for robust quality control to maintain high yields and reliability in wafer production. In this context, accurately predicting wafer failures plays a pivotal role across the industry in minimizing production losses and enhancing cost efficiency. However, despite the use of traditional machine learning and deep learning methods to predict wafer failures, they have failed to achieve the desired levels of accuracy. Consequently, the present study investigates the application of Quantum Machine Learning (QML) methods on the SECOM dataset. This dataset was balanced using the Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique (SMOTE), wherein the QML models were implemented using the PennyLane library. In this study, comprehensive data pre-processing was performed on the SECOM dataset; subsequently, various QML algorithms such as Quantum Support Vector Machines (QSVM) and Quantum Random Forests (QRF) were implemented to classify wafers as ‘good’ or ‘bad.’ Although initial improvements in performance compared to traditional methods were modest, leveraging PennyLane’s capabilities and fundamental principles of QML, this study highlights their transformative potential for industrial applications.

titles.title: Quantum-enhanced wafer failure prediction in semiconductor fabrication

abstracts.value: We formulate the dissipation due to sound-wave emission from a Keplerian binary embedded in a homogeneous Newtonian fluid background at rest in the binary center-of-mass frame within linear perturbation theory. Rather than starting from the local wake force, we treat the binary as a localized periodic mass source and compute the sound-wave fluxes carried away by the medium. The time-averaged energy, linear-momentum, and angular-momentum fluxes are obtained from Noether currents of the fluid perturbations. For a classical inviscid barotropic Newtonian fluid, retaining the self-gravity of density perturbations while adopting the Jeans prescription, we derive explicit flux formulas for circular and eccentric binaries with arbitrary mass ratio. This formulation also clarifies the ultraviolet behavior of point sources: in a nondispersive fluid, the harmonic sum becomes cutoff-sensitive precisely when at least one component becomes supersonic. We examine explicitly how finite source size removes this divergence using a uniform-sphere model and relate the resulting regularization to a corresponding effective harmonic cutoff. The associated secular eccentricity evolution exhibits circularization in the subsonic regime when the fluid self-gravity is sufficiently weak but can change sign outside this regime, with eccentricity growth in the strictly supersonic UV limit. For a Schrödinger-Poisson quantum fluid, quantum pressure instead softens the high-frequency contribution and renders the point-source fluxes UV finite within the nonrelativistic regime; our numerical results further indicate eccentricity growth due to sound radiation over the parameter space explored. Finally, we translate orbital-decay measurements of two binary pulsars into order-of-magnitude bounds on the homogeneous quantum-fluid density surrounding each system.

titles.title: Sound of Keplerian binaries in a homogeneous Newtonian fluid background

abstracts.value: We derive a microscopic relation between the many-body Chern number $C$ of the fermionic ground state and the braiding of fluxes in $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ gauge theory coupled to matter: under a spectral gap condition, dressed flux loops obey $W_2W_1=e^{i\fracπ{2}C}W_1W_2$ on the ground-state sector. We realize $C=1$ by gauging charge parity in a weakly interacting Qi-Wu-Zhang insulator. Reflection positivity and chessboard estimates show that flux defects are massive, which yields a gapped, topologically ordered phase with four locally indistinguishable ground states.

abstracts.value: Classical electrodynamics exhibits an elegant symmetry known as electromagnetic duality invariance, which reflects the covariance of the free Maxwell equations under continuous SO(2) transformations that mix the electric and magnetic fields. However, the standard Lagrangian formulation does not natively incorporate this symmetry. Furthermore, the linear Maxwell model is limited by the issue of self-interaction energy divergences for point charges. To restore this symmetry at the level of the variational action and resolve the problem of classical divergences, non-linear extensions of electrodynamics have been formulated. These include the well-known Born-Infeld theory, which is of particular modern interest due to its connections with string theory and D-branes.This work critically analyzes and compares the main formal frameworks developed in the literature to generate non-linear Lagrangians for the electromagnetic field in a four-dimensional spacetime that intrinsically incorporate duality invariance.

titles.title: Estensioni non lineari e invarianti per dualità dell’elettrodinamica classica

Abstract: We study specific subclasses of non-twisting geometries in the context of
quadratic gravity using the Newman–Penrose and Geroch–Held–Penrose formalisms.
The main result is the derivation of the linearised field equations of quadratic gravity
within these frame formalisms. The resulting constraints on linear perturbations are
expressed entirely through the Ricci tensor projections, reducing the problem from
fourth-order equations in metric functions to a second-order system of differential
equations for the curvature. Additionally, a new exact spherically symmetric solution of
quadratic gravity with a cosmological constant is presented in the fully explicit form.
The results provide a foundation for future stability analysis and quasinormal mode
studies of black holes in quadratic gravity.

Keywords: gravity, general relativity, null tetrad, quadratic gravity, black holes, gravita-
tional waves, differential geometry

Introduction
Despite this work being theoretical, we use this introduction as a place to com-

ment on the connection to the experimental side of gravity. The first observation of
the gravitational-wave signal was GW150914 by a pair of detectors of the Laser In-
terferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO) in 2015 [1], and the new age of
astronomical observations began. The signal was produced by the merger of binary
black-hole system and as such it can not only carry the information about the parameters
of the black holes participating in the merger, but also about underlying theory itself, e.g.,
the propagation speed of the modes [2] or the second law of thermodynamics of black
holes [3]. So far, general relativity (GR) has described the gravitational signal of the
merger of black holes well [4]. However, with the next generations of gravitational-wave
detectors, the measurement precisions will increase, and remnants of the strong-field
regime are expected to surpass GR. These discrepancies will help us to understand the
gravitational theory on a more fundamental level. The aim of this thesis is to deepen
our understanding of theories extending GR. The thesis is organised as follows.

In Chapter 1, we elaborate a little on why there exists a pursuit for theories beyond
GR, but the means by which to do it is exactly through the gravitational waves. Many
techniques have been developed to do so. Particularly interesting is the study of the
quasinormal modes. These modes are present during the final stage, the ring down, of the
binary merger [5]. One of the ways how to obtain them is via the process of linearisation
of the field equations. Note that this is also how the gravitational waves were originally
predicted [6]. The common way towards the linear perturbations is within the metric
formulation [7]. However, this approach becomes vastly complicated for more involved
backgrounds. That is why another perspective on the geometry was employed. Instead of
using the metric tensor explicitly, it is convenient to introduce a null tetrad of vectors, in
which the metric is implicitly encoded. The so-called Newman–Penrose (NP) formalism
[8, 9] then rewrites the tensorial quantities as scalars, which presents a conceptual shift
in the description of geometry. The basics of this language are summarised in Chapter 2.
The NP formalism, as a useful mathematical tool, was used by Teukolsky to study the
linear perturbations on the Kerr background [10, 11], which represents a very realistic
and astrophysical setting. He managed to separate the differential equations governing
the perturbations and reduce the complexity of the problem to solving the second-order
ordinary differential equations for each mode.

The NP formalism also offers a geometric insight into the theory. In particular, the
Petrov classification [12], which is based on the classification of the Weyl curvature
tensor, is elegant in the language of the NP Weyl scalars. The main idea of the classifica-
tion is the construction of the tetrad to coincide with so-called principal null directions,
that is, the directions in which the Weyl tensor vanishes. More detailed interpretation is
discussed in Sec. 2.5. Another important NP scalars are the Ricci rotation coefficients,
which represent the change of the null tetrad in a point of spacetime. The most geomet-
rically transparent Ricci rotation coefficients are those describing the null congruences
generated by the null vectors of the tetrad. In particular, change in the null direction can
be interpreted as the deformation of the optical rays. Then the behaviour of the optical
rays can be described by their expansion, shear, and twist. In Chapter 3, we rewrite
important geometries in the NP formalism to build a geometric interpretation of the NP
scalars and use them as backgrounds for perturbations.

11



The aim of this thesis is to use the NP (or later Geroch–Held–Penrose (GHP))
formalism to formulate the linear perturbations in a modified theory of gravity, quadratic
gravity. The explicit perturbed field equation system with its derivation is presented in
Chapter 4. The field equations are written as the second order differential equations
for the Ricci curvature scalars as the unknown functions depending on the spacetime
coordinates. Such a formulation is useful for both theoretical point of view for studying
stability of quadratic gravity, but also for the experimental side of gravity since, for
example, the field equations in this form can be studied to obtain the quasinormal modes
of black holes.

In the last part, Chapter 5, we focus on specific exact solutions of quadratic gravity.
Exact solutions as such are in general a good benchmark to perturbation theory and
provide a controlled environment in which various ideas can be tested. Exact solutions
are very rare even in GR. Obtaining a new exact solution in quadratic gravity that is not
present in GR is significantly more difficult. Here, we present such a solution, which
is of spherical symmetry and couples with the cosmological constant. Moreover, we
examine spherical symmetry more generally with Frobenius analysis in a new coordinate
system and relate it to previous work [13, 14].

1 Modified theories of gravity
General relativity (GR), as a fundamental theory of gravity, has remained mostly

unchanged since its formulation [15] and is to this day the most accurate description of the
gravitational interaction. Together with the standard model of particle physics, it forms
a foundation of contemporary fundamental physics. It has been speculated for a long
time that GR cannot be a universal gravitational theory, and many modifications were
introduced early on [16, 17]. The main arguments are both theoretical and experimental.

The former usually includes extensive discussions of the existence of singularities
in the theory and their nature, renormalizability of the theory and UV completeness or
even interaction of the classical gravitational field with quantum fields [18]. Several
ideas were used to overcome these difficulties such as the framework of the quantum
field theory, higher-derivative theories, string theory, or loop quantum gravity.

On the experimental side, the accelerated expansion of the universe was a big surprise
that led to accepting the cosmological constant Λ to the theory as the source of dark
energy causing the accelerated expansion of the universe. However, its fundamental
nature remains unclear. There are also discrepancies on the level of galaxies and galaxy
clusters, and thus dark matter was introduced. On the other hand, there exist more
possibilities to go beyond GR than to introduce the dark universe.

To begin with, when talking about modifications, we need to present what action
is to be modified. The action that produces the Einstein field equations of GR is the
Einstein–Hilbert action,

1.1 Higher dimensional theories
The standard playground for GR is the (3 + 1)-dimensional manifold, where the

number 3 refers to the space-like dimensions, and the number 1 is the time-like dimension.
Naturally, one can play with this setup. For example, string theories are said to work in
10 (and more) dimensions. Then, the number of dimensions D can be kept arbitrary.
However, in order to describe the physical reality, the additional dimensions need to
be somehow hidden (compactified) on a wide range of scales. For example, taking
into account the Newtonian potential, the point-like source generates the potential with
the radial dependance r−(D−3), but stable planetary orbits require D = 4. Still, it is
interesting to look at other caveats of general dimension.

An interesting approach to higher-dimensional theories is the limit of large dimen-
sions to study a black-hole horizon and its potential quantum gravitational effects [20].
Due to the existence of black-hole solutions and the propagation of degrees of freedom
in D ≥ 4, one can investigate properties in the limit D →∞, where some calculations
are expected to be more manageable.

13



On the other hand, we can consider lower dimensions, e.g., 2+1 dimensional gravity.
It was shown that in this setup, gravity is perturbatively renormalizable [21] and the
action has the form of the Chern–Simons action, which is in fact a gauge theory and can
be obtained as an expansion of string theories [22]. For more information, see [23].

The key aspect of the 2 + 1 setting is that the curvature is fully determined by the
field equations since the Riemann and Ricci tensors possess the same number of degrees
of freedom. Thus, the dynamics is essentially different (or lacking) in that sense that the
vacuum solutions are strictly Minkowski or (anti-)de Sitter. More on the solutions in
2 + 1 gravity in [24].

1.2 Theories with additional fields
The natural way to extend GR is to introduce additional matter fields in the gravi-

tational sector. The simplest choice would be a scalar field commonly denoted φ, but
other choices such as vectors and rank-2 tensors are common too. An important part
(not only) of these theories is a screening mechanism, which suppresses the effects of
the novel fields on the well established GR scale, e.g., weak coupling.

1.2.3 Tensor-vector-scalar theories
The tensor-vector-scalar (TeVeS) theories contain both a scalar field φ and a vector

field Aa. A review of these types of theories can be found in [36]. This type of
theories is relevant because they introduce the covariant completion of MOND (Sec. 1.3).
Despite MOND’s success in explaining galactic rotation curves, it can hardly be applied
in cosmological settings, since it is a non-relativistic gravitational theory. Bekenstein,
extending the work of Sanders in the TeVeS, proposed a relativistic (TeVeS) theory with
a MOND limit for non-relativistic systems.

The gravitational part of the action in the TeVeS theory is split into gravitational
part Sg̃, vector part SA, and a scalar part Sφ, see [19],

S = Sg̃ + SA + Sφ , (1.5)

where g̃ is the so-called Bekenstein metric. The transformation to the physical metric g
is

gab = e−2φg̃ab − 2AaAb sinh 2φ . (1.6)

1.4 Higher-derivative theories
Higher-derivative theories, as a subclass of modified theories, are subject to ghosts

too. When talking about these ghosts in modified theories, we mean physical degrees of
freedom that come with modifications of gravity, this is in contrast to the case of the
Faddeev–Popov ghost, which is the result of the process of quantisation of non-abelian
fields. The physical ghosts can mediate an additional repulsive force, which is connected
to the different sign of the kinetic term, e.g. (1.38) — also see [19] — which results in
energies unbounded from below. Let us elaborate on some important higher-derivative
theories, namely, f(R) theory [38] and the Stelle quadratic gravity [39, 40].

The quantities in question are the Ricci tensor Rab and the Weyl tensor Cabcd, as well as
the derivatives of the tetrad itself. Vectors of the frame are often adapted for a symmetry
of the spacetime, and thus allow expressions to be simplified considerably. Additionally,
there is a conceptual shift to try to abandon non-physical coordinate-related degrees of
freedom and arrive at more invariant quantities.

In this chapter, we offer an outline of the NP and GHP formalisms from the construc-
tion of the null tetrad, introduction of the Ricci rotation coefficients and their connection
to the torsion, through the formulation of the curvature and related identities, and last
but not least, the differential operators that are commonly used.

2.1 Null tetrad and related quantities

Firstly, let us introduce what the null tetrad (k, l,m, m̄) actually is. The vectors k
and l are future-oriented null vectors, i.e.,

k · k = l · l = 0 , k · l = −1 , (2.2)

and m is a spacelike complex vector1 with the complex conjugation denoted as m̄.
Naturally, the spacelike vector m is perpendicular to the null directions

k ·m = l ·m = m ·m = 0 , (2.3)

and satisfies standard complex normalisation,

m · m̄ = 1 . (2.4)

In that case, any metric g of the four-dimensional Lorentzian manifold can be decom-
posed into these four directions (k, l,m, m̄) in the following way,

g = −kl− lk +mm̄+ m̄m . (2.5)

The graphical representation of the null tetrad is visualised in Fig. 2.1.

2.5 Petrov classification

The null rotations (2.95) or (2.96) naturally transform the Weyl scalars resulting in
the fourth-order algebraic equation in complex variable parametrising such a rotation
in the case we want to obtain a specific value of Ψ4 or Ψ0, respectively. Taking the latter
(Eq. (2.96)), the transformation of the Weyl scalar Ψ0 is (see [49]),

Ψ0 → Ψ0 + 4EΨ1 + 6E2Ψ2 + 4E3Ψ3 + E4Ψ4 . (2.103)

The vector k is said to be a principal null direction (PND) if the corresponding Weyl
scalar Ψ0 vanishes,

Ψ0 = 0 . (2.104)

By the fundamental theorem of algebra, the transformation given by Eq. (2.103) has
exactly four roots including multiplicities, that is, the Weyl tensor has exactly four PNDs
including multiplicities. The Petrov type is determined by the coincidence pattern of
these roots.

Petrov type multiplicities description

I (1, 1, 1, 1) algebraically general
II (2, 1, 1) one repeated PND
III (3, 1) one triply repeated PND
D (2, 2) two repeated PNDs
N (4) one quadruply repeated PND
O conformally flat spacetime

The degeneration of the PND is well represented by the Penrose diagram depicted in
Fig. 2.2. Individual arrows represent the increase in the multiplicity of a particular PND.

30



Figure 2.2 The Penrose diagram of the degeneracy of the PND.

Since the Weyl scalars enter various expressions within this thesis, for example, as
backgrounds in the perturbations, we shall briefly discuss the physical interpretation of
the special Petrov types.

2.5.1 Type II – one repeated PND
There is one double-degenerate PND present. The gravitational field has a preferred

null direction with the enhanced symmetry. Radiation and Coulomb-like components
coexist, but the repeated PND behaves differently from the two simple ones. The
structure of the Weyl scalars using such a frame component is

Ψ0 = Ψ1 = 0 , Ψ2,Ψ3,Ψ4 ̸= 0 . (2.105)

The typical example of GR exact spacetimes of this type is gravitational waves propa-
gating on type D backgrounds [52].

2.5.2 Type D – two repeated PNDs
The D stands for ‘degenerate’ since there are two doubly-repeated PNDs. It is very

common that the black holes are of this type, e.g., the Schwarzschild, Kerr, Reissner–
Nordström and other black-hole solutions [52]. The Goldberg–Sachs theorem [53, 54]
guarantees the PNDs are geodesic and shear-free. This leads directly to the separabil-
ity of the Hamilton–Jacobi, Klein–Gordon, Dirac, and Teukolsky equations on these
backgrounds. The structure of the Weyl scalars in such a case is

Ψ0 = Ψ1 = Ψ3 = Ψ4 = 0 , Ψ2 ̸= 0 . (2.106)

2.5.3 Type III – one triply repeated PND
In contrast to the previous case, in this type there is a longitudinal gravitational field

present. The structure of the Weyl scalars is

Ψ0 = Ψ1 = Ψ2 = 0 , Ψ3,Ψ4 ̸= 0 . (2.107)

The typical examples include gyratons. For more, see [52, 39].

31



2.5.4 Type N – quadruply repeated PND
Such a spacetime is commonly interpreted as a gravitational wave. There is only

one preferred null direction and that correspond to the direction of the null transversal
radiation in that spacetime. The structure of the Weyl scalars is

Ψ0 = Ψ1 = Ψ2 = Ψ3 = 0 , Ψ4 ̸= 0 . (2.108)

The typical GR type N spacetimes belong to the Kundt or Robinson–Trautman (RT)
class; see [52].

2.5.5 Type O – conformally flat spacetime
In the conformally flat spacetime, the Weyl tensor vanishes entirely. Such spacetimes

include de Sitter, anti-de Sitter, and Minkowski geometry i.e., maximally symmetric
spacetimes.

3 Non-twisting geometries
In the previous chapter, namely in Sec. 2.1.1, we introduced the Ricci rotation

coefficients. Usage of these coefficients is convenient, because they are directly related
to the physical interpretation of the investigated spacetime. Some of them inherently
describe the behaviour of the null tetrad and the associated null curves in the spacetime.
In particular, the null field is often interpreted as tangents of the optical rays — null
geodesics generated by the null vector field, e.g., k — whose possible deformations
are expansion Θ, twist A, and shear σ. Thus, these properties are encoded in the Ricci
rotation coefficients (2.11)–(2.18), see [49], namely geodesicity in the coefficients κ
(see Eq. (3.20) of Sec. 3.2),

κ = 0 , (3.1)
expansion Θ and twist A in the coefficient ρ,

and finally shear σ is directly denoted as the Ricci rotation coefficient σ (2.13). Naturally,
the condition for the non-twisting geometry is A = 0, which gives

ρ = ρ̄ , (3.3)

i.e., the Ricci rotation coefficient ρ is real. In the following section, we shall discuss
two important classes of geometries that satisfy such conditions, that is, spherically
symmetric settings and the near-horizon extremal Kerr metric, which is of the Kundt
type; see below.

The historically prominent classes of non-twisting geometries are the Kundt class
[56] and the Robinson–Trautman (RT) class [57, 58]. The Kundt class is more restrictive
in the sense that it sets all the optical scalars to zero, i.e.,

A = 0 , σ = 0 , ρ = 0 , (3.4)

while the RT class keeps the expansion Θ non-vanishing,

A = 0 , σ = 0 , ρ = −Θ . (3.5)

These geometric properties and related aspects are discussed below.

3.4 Spherical symmetry
Spherical symmetry represents an important and non-trivial constraint on the geom-

etry that is employed very often within investigating various theories of gravity. That
is because while the spherical symmetry is relatively restrictive, it still possesses rich
classes of solutions, especially in modified theories, as black holes, wormholes, naked
singularities, etc. Two natural questions that arise in the context of the modified theories
are whether the Schwarzschild solution is still the solution of the vacuum field equations
and whether this solution is still unique, i.e., the only spherically symmetric solution of
the vacuum field equations.

3.5 Kerr metric
The Kerr metric [65] describes the geometry of a stationary axially symmetric

rotating black hole with the mass M and the rotation parameter a. It solves the vacuum
Einstein equations with vanishing cosmological constant (Λ = 0), thus, the scalar
curvature R and the Ricci tensor Rab are identically zero, i.e., the Kerr spacetime is an
Einstein space, which means that the Bach tensor Bab is vanishing as well.

adapted frame [66, 67, 68]. Additionally, the near horizon geometry of Sec. 3.6 is of

various matter contents, namely the electromagnetic or neutrino fields as sources for the
perturbations, or just effects of vacuum dynamical gravitational field. Interestingly, in
GR the equations for such fields decouple completely. In quadratic gravity, the motivation
is similar, our goal is to obtain the field equations for the dynamical gravitational field in
the Kerr background. In the following 11 pages, the Phys. Rev. D version of the paper

Employing the Newman-Penrose formalism and following the classic Teukolsky-like approach, we

linearize the field equations of quadratic gravity on the Kerr background and combine them with the

linearized Ricci and Bianchi identities. This leads to constraints on linear perturbations of the Kerr

spacetime in quadratic gravity. The resulting differential equations are decoupled in such a way that only

the Ricci tensor perturbations need to be found on the Kerr background in order to fully determine the

solution. The results are illustrated in the simple nontrivial cases of the Schwarzschild and Minkowski

geometries.

I. INTRODUCTION

The idea of modifying general relativity (GR) has been

reflected for a long time, beginning immediately after the

formulation of GR [1,2] and extending to the present day;

see, e.g., [3]. In general, we can conclude that modifica-

tions of GR are inevitable either from an observational

point of view [4,5] or from a purely theoretical perspective

[6,7]. The latter is concerned mainly with the ways of

extending GR in the strong-field regime. The natural way

of modifying GR is to introduce additional higher-curva-

ture terms to the Einstein-Hilbert action. This can be argued

as an effective field theory method. Namely, the quadratic

curvature terms, whose effects are investigated in this

paper, make the theory renormalizable [8] but the price

paid is to introduce so-called ghosts in the theory. These

ghosts propagate additional degrees of freedom, that is,

massive spin-0 and massive spin-2 mediators connected to

the presence of up to the fourth-order derivatives. Although

problematic, it is prospectively causal [9], and the physi-

cally relevant consequences can still be derived below the

cutoff energy scale.

The (Stelle) quadratic gravity [10] investigated in this

paper contains two prominent subclasses. One of them is

R2-theory that was of interest in the cosmological models

of inflation; see, e.g., [11]. The second one, Einstein-Weyl

gravity, extends the GR action by the square of the Weyl

tensor. Interestingly, it was shown that the gravitational

effects of the Weyl (spin-2) term can exceed those of the R2

(spin-0) in the case of compact stars [12].

The interesting and well-reasoned settings for studying

quadratic gravity implications are black holes. The astro-

physically most relevant case is represented by the Kerr

spacetime [13], which describes the geometry of a sta-

tionary axially symmetric rotating black hole. This setting

is shown to be the only GR stable rotating solution which is

astrophysically viable. Thus, there is much focus on finding

remnants of strong-field gravity extending GR in the Kerr

background, such as gravitational wave analysis [14] or

black-hole images [15]. Although available data are in

agreement with the Kerr properties, much is unknown with

respect to possible tiny discrepancies described by alter-

native theories. Here, Stelle’s quadratic gravity is a natural

candidate since the GR vacuum spacetimes themselves also

solve the field equations of quadratic gravity and thus

provide suitable backgrounds for perturbative analysis.

The perturbative approach is also closely related to the

study of spacetime stability, which is an important topic not

only in GR but also has been gaining interest within

modified gravity theories during the past years. For

example, starting with the Schwarzschild solution and

spherical perturbations, it was shown that small-mass black

holes (compared to theory constants) are unstable within

quadratic gravity [16]. A similar conclusion also holds for

the alternative branch of non-Schwarzschild spherically

symmetric black holes [17]. More recently, the nonradial

perturbations of spherically symmetric black holes were

studied in [18,19].

We aim to follow Teukolsky’s approach [20], where the

Newman-Penrose (NP) scalar quantities [21] are perturbed

rather than the metric coefficients. In general, this allows

one to perform a coordinate-independent analysis of the

perturbative modes. The NP formalism permits placing the

additional conditions on the perturbations, e.g., their

algebraic structure, existence and behavior of null geodesic

IV. SUMMARY

As our main result, we derive the differential equa-

tions (32) and (33)–(38) that constrain arbitrary perturba-

tions of the Kerr background governed by a generic

quadratic theory of gravity and can serve further in various

applications. All perturbations are encoded in terms of the

Ricci tensor projections. In general, we employ the

Newman-Penrose formalism, which provides the advantage

of coordinate-independent statements. Simultaneously, the

differential equations are of the second order, and thus their

analysis could become easier in comparison with the

fourth-order constraints in terms of the metric functions.

Moreover, the Ricci tensor projections, and subsequently

related Newman-Penrose scalars, can be connected to

physically relevant quantities, and specific viable assump-

tions can thus be directly performed with respect to a

particular situation to be described, e.g., algebraic structure,

behavior of test observers, spacetime symmetries, etc.

Finally, the Kerr background itself, as a vacuum solution

to general relativity, does not contribute to the Ricci

curvature, and thus its any nontrivial part immediately

arises as the quadratic gravity correction and can easily be

recognized.

As simple examples, the static radial perturbations of the

Minkowski and Schwarzschild geometries were presented

using this approach. However, a much more interesting and

technically challenging discussion of perturbations as, e.g.,

extension of complete Kerr spacetime within quadratic

gravity or effects of matter and dynamics even for simpler

backgrounds are postponed for further work. Also, a

similar stability analysis to that carried out in [18,19] will

be interesting starting with the Kerr background. Moreover,

in [33], an approximative slowly rotating black hole was

studied, concluding that two branches of solutions exist, the

classic Kerr branch and the additional quadratic-gravity

one. Investigating such a possibility within the presented

formalism could also give a deeper insight into the structure

of such solutions.

5 Exact solutions
Exact solutions of any theory of gravity occupy the privileged position in studying

the theory itself. Investigating such solutions reinforces the understanding of its fun-
damentals and improves the physical intuition in general. It is not surprising that the
exact solutions are as important in modified theories of gravity as in GR [49, 52]. Over
more than century, the well-known Schwarzschild solution [61] has demonstrated how
crucial an exact solution can be in the development of a theory. Here, the Schwarzschild
solution is mentioned also for the second reason and that is the underlying geometric
assumption, i.e., spherical symmetry. Although the axial symmetry of the Kerr solution
is more realistic, the increase in complexity of the solution is significant. Additionally,
higher-derivative theories bring new layers of challenges, so spherically symmetric ge-
ometries are prominently investigated as highly relevant spacetimes not only in quadratic
gravity.

5.1 Frobenius analysis of the exact solutions

allows more types of solutions [13, 45, 14, 46, 47]. The way these results were primarily

or the Frobenius analysis. In the last case, the assumption is that the solution of the
field equations can be expanded in a form of power series in a ‘radial’ variable of the
coordinate system used in the calculation.

5.3 Exact Bachian singularity in quadratic gravity
(paper)

So far, in this chapter, only power series form of the solutions have been presented.
Surprisingly, there is also a fully explicit solution in terms of powers of radial coordinates
that does not need infinite series. It was presented in [74], Š. Knoška, D. Kofroň, and
R. Švarc, Exact Bachian singularity in quadratic gravity, Phys. Rev. D 113 124020
(2026). The downside is that it requires very fine-tuned parameters. Still, having the
exact solution in a compact form offers an insightful playground for analysis of quadratic
gravity in spherical symmetry. In the next 13 pages the Phys. Rev. D version of the
paper follows.

For specifically coupled values of the quadratic gravity parameters, we present a fully explicit static
spherically symmetric solution. It contains the central singularity surrounded by the black-hole or the
cosmological horizon for the negative or positive cosmological parameter, respectively. This spacetime,
thus, belongs to the already analyzed classes of solutions expressed in terms of the Frobenius expansions,
continuous fractions, or numerical simulations; however, it has not been explicitly identified before. The
purpose of the presented highly constrained somehow unphysical model is to reveal a global geometric
picture that may occur in spherical spacetimes within quadratic gravity, which is typically hidden in more
general approximative solutions. At the same time, it can serve as a solid benchmark for evaluating the
accuracy of the methods employed to obtain such solutions.

I. INTRODUCTION

Modified theories of gravity have garnered considerable
attention over the past decade [1–4]. This follows from both
practical reasons for explaining observational phenomena
[5] and theoretical reasons for discovering mysteries of the
quantum theory of gravity. For the latter case, it is natural to
allow the quadratic terms in curvature to be present in the
action because these terms naturally arise from the semi-
classical limit of quantum stringlike theories. Additionally,
such action is renormalizable with the drawback of intro-
ducing ghosts into the theory [6].
The physically reasonable and natural setting to test the

consequences of quadratic gravity is to assume a static and
spherically symmetric spacetime. This allows us to study
generalizations of the classic Schwarzschild geometry [7].
Surprisingly, in contrast to the Birkhoff theorem in general
relativity (GR), many other (non-)black-hole solutions are
present in this setup [8–15] in addition to the Schwarzschild
one. Moreover, even with the restrictive spherical assu-
mption, the generalized non-Schwarzschild solutions with
the quadratic contribution present cannot be typically
expressed in terms of elementary functions, and various
techniques to obtain such solutions are employed, namely,
the Frobenius-like analysis of the power series, numerical
integration, or linearization of the equations in the weak-
field regime.

One of the most important questions discussed is the
asymptotic behavior of the black-hole solutions and
whether the asymptotically flat (black-hole) solution with
the Schwarzschild limit can even exist. This was inves-
tigated, e.g., in [8,9,16,17], and others. It was shown that
asymptotically flat black holes are very special. In fact, they
require some fine-tuning of the parameters.
As we have already mentioned, quadratic theory in the

spherically symmetric regime is richer than in GR and
allows for qualitatively different types of solutions. This
means that another important task is to identify and classify
all possible solutions. The detailed classification was carried
out using the conformal-to-Kundt coordinates [18] in [15].
These coordinates offer a surprisingly simple formulation of
the quadratic gravity field equations. However, the classi-
fication is not necessarily complete because it is based on
power series expansions, which are coordinate-dependent.
In particular, some coordinates do not allow the power series
expansion of a specific solution. Moreover, the Frobenius-
like solutions are limited by the convergence radii of the
series and can thus describe only the local behavior of the
geometry rather than its global structure.
Due to the complexity of quadratic gravity and the

richness of its solution space, even in the simple case of
spherical symmetry [19], its deeper understanding remains
an open problem. Therefore, the analysis of a fully explicit
global exact solution, which will be carried out in this
paper, seems very interesting, even though the price to pay
is a very specific coupling of the theory constants.
The paper is organized as follows: in the remaining part

of the Introduction, we summarize the description of
quadratic gravity and spherically symmetric geometries.
